nodes.title: Working with the specification
nodes.text: How the specification is kept and implemented.

children.title: The foundations
children.text: The principles that every other rule of the guidelines refines, in the order in which a change passes through them: the node, the rule, its approval, its test and its code, with the checks holding the whole path together.

decisions.problem: The section was titled "The model", which said neither what it holds nor that its rules are not the specification itself but those it is kept by.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the section is titled "The foundations": it holds the rules every other section rests on, what the specification is made of and how it is changed. A title naming the approach was weighed and set aside as longer than needed.

children.title: The specification
children.text: What the specification is and what it consists of.

children.title: The specification is the set of its nodes
children.text: The specification is the set of its nodes. The nodes are arranged in a structure. Where needed, a node also refers to other nodes through links of various types.
children.reason: The structure of the specification and the links between its nodes help in understanding the context and the dependencies of each node.

decisions.problem: The node said only that the specification is the set of its nodes, and nothing about how the nodes relate to one another.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the node also says that the nodes are arranged in a structure. Where needed, a node refers to other nodes through links of various types.

decisions.problem: The reason was about the copies generated from the nodes, which this node no longer mentions.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the reason says that the structure and the links between the nodes help in understanding each node's context and dependencies.

decisions.problem: The text said that the nodes are "linked to one another by a structure", although the structure is not a link. It also said that a node "links to" other nodes, which is appropriate only for a strict link.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the nodes are "arranged in a structure", since the word "link" is reserved for the links between nodes. A node "refers to" other nodes, since a link may also be a loose one.

children.title: The basic structure of the specification
children.reason:
The parts change at different rates. The guidelines hardly change. The base specification changes with the system's business logic or its core functionality. The technical appendix changes most often.

The rules of one subject area bear on one another and change together, so they are kept together. With the appendix divided the same way as the base, there is only one place to look for a rule's implementation.

decisions.problem: The item on the guidelines did not state precisely what they cover.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the guidelines say how the specification is kept and implemented.

decisions.problem: The node did not say whether the base specification may be divided, or how the technical appendix is structured if it is.
decisions.ruling: The owner: where needed, the base specification may be divided. If it is, the technical appendix inherits the structure of the base specification where the two overlap.

decisions.problem: The reason said that the base specification is divided because a specification may grow too large.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the division is not driven by size, so the reason does not mention size.

decisions.problem: The node mentioned domains, which are defined by an extension of the guidelines that a project may not have chosen.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the rules that every project shares do not name domains. The mention is removed, and the rule's meaning stays the same.

children.title: What the guidelines govern
children.text: The guidelines say how the specification is built and by which rules it must be written. A particular project may extend the rules of the guidelines but cannot change them.
children.reason: If the rules of the guidelines are changed, the tools that check the format and the implementation against the guidelines will stop working correctly.

decisions.problem: The node was written before the rules of one thought to a sentence (s-juucyammgq4shq8) and of what is applied together (s-6j8ystpj2yzcchq), and before the names of the method were settled.
decisions.ruling: In the owner's name, carrying out those rules and the names the owner settled on 2026-11-07: the wording rewritten, its meaning unchanged.

decisions.problem: The title referred to the whole specification, although the node is only about the guidelines.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the title names the guidelines.

decisions.problem: The node did not say whether a project may change the rules of the guidelines.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a project may extend the rules of the guidelines but cannot change them. Changed rules would stop the tools that check the format and the implementation against the guidelines from working correctly.

decisions.problem: The node also listed the cases in which a rule is dropped.
decisions.ruling: The owner: that list and its reason move to the section on how a rule is written.

children.title: What the base specification states
children.text:
A rule of the base specification (§s-qmmzf9nksfsa3qp) states what the system does: the business logic to be implemented. It may also contain any further business information needed to understand the rule precisely, with all its nuances and edge cases.

A rule of the base specification names a technology as follows:
- a technology that the system is built with, only as an example, in parentheses, where the rule is independent of it;
- a technology that is part of what the system does, such as a protocol it speaks or a format it accepts, in the same way as anything else the rule states, even where the system is also built with it.
children.reason: The base specification is meant to outlive the technology stack: the system can be rebuilt on another stack, with another version of the technical appendix, without editing a single rule. A technology that is part of what the system does stays the same on every stack, so naming it makes no rule go stale.
examples: A service accepts payment orders as XML messages in a format a standard defines. Every implementation must accept that format, so the base specification names it. The most likely mistake is a rule that also names the library that parses these messages, a technology the service is built with. A project's own guidelines may refine the rule in this node by listing the technologies that the project's base specification names.

decisions.problem: One rule held what the base names of a technology, of a look and of one instance, and grew too long to read as one requirement.
decisions.ruling: The owner: three rules, one for each.

decisions.problem: The node was written before the rules of one thought to a sentence (s-juucyammgq4shq8) and of what is applied together (s-6j8ystpj2yzcchq), and before the names of the method were settled.
decisions.ruling: In the owner's name, carrying out those rules and the names the owner settled on 2026-11-07: the wording rewritten, its meaning unchanged.

decisions.problem: The node was framed as a ban: its title and part of its text said what a rule of the base specification does not name.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the node says what a rule of the base specification states, namely the business logic and any further business information needed to understand the rule precisely. The list of what such a rule does not name is removed, as is the sentence that repeated what the node on the technical appendix says.

decisions.problem: The reason did not say that the base specification can be implemented on another stack.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the reason says that the system can be rebuilt on another stack, with another version of the technical appendix, without editing a single rule.

decisions.problem: The node barred the base specification from naming any technology, even one that is part of what the system does.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a technology that the system is built with is named only as an example, in parentheses. A technology that is part of what the system does, such as a protocol it speaks or a format it accepts, is named like anything else the rule states.

children.title: The technical appendix describes how the rules are implemented
children.text: The technical appendix describes how the rules of the base specification are to be implemented. It also contains all the technical detail needed: the system's stack, how each part of the system is built and how the user interface looks. It describes them in as much detail as an agent needs to implement them.
children.reason: How a rule is implemented has no other home, since the base specification names a technology that the system is built with only as an example. Described less precisely, it would leave a choice to whoever implements it. That choice would then be recorded in the code, not in the specification.

decisions.problem: The node that names the three parts of the specification was not followed by a node on each part.
decisions.ruling: The owner: each of the three parts is described in a node of its own, right after the node that names them. This node describes the technical appendix.

decisions.problem: The node did not say clearly whose needs set the level of detail in the technical appendix.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the technical appendix describes the implementation in as much detail as an agent needs to implement the rules.

decisions.problem: The node mentioned domains, which are defined by an extension of the guidelines that a project may not have chosen.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the rules that every project shares do not name domains. The mention is removed, and the rule's meaning stays the same.

decisions.problem: The reason relied on the base specification naming no technology at all, which no longer holds.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the reason says that the implementation of a rule has no other home, since the base specification names the technologies the system is built with only as examples.

children.title: The owners
children.text: The whole specification must have an owner, responsible for approving its nodes. Each part may be assigned an owner of its own. There may be several owners. A part's owners take the place of the owners at the level above for every node within it.
children.reason: The owners are those accountable for a rule and approve it (§s-67vekyup7y8smap). A node is implemented only once it is approved. Owners of sections divide the reading as the specification is divided, so that it can grow beyond what one person can read. The owners of one part share the work of reading it. Each of them is accountable for all of it.

decisions.problem: The rule on owners stood after rules that already relied on the notion of an owner.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the rule moves ahead of them, so that the notion of an owner is introduced before it is first used.

tests: skills/tools/test/unit/model.test.ts::@spec s-6sk8uet75dmq5qz names no owner where the specification names none
skills/tools/test/unit/model.test.ts::@spec s-6sk8uet75dmq5qz takes a node's owners from the nearest section or header that names owners, otherwise from the specification's owners

children.title: The rule
children.text: What a rule is and what it holds.

children.title: One node, one rule
children.text: A node contains only one numbered rule. All the parts that make up the rule — paragraphs, tables and code blocks — belong to that node rather than to nodes beside it.
children.reason: A rule's parts only make sense together. Splitting them into nodes of their own would create a second set of locations for fragments nothing can cite.

children.title: A node is cited by its sid
children.text: A node of the specification has a sid, given to it once and never changed. A node, and so the rule it holds, is cited by its sid everywhere: in the links between nodes, in the code, in the tests and in commits.
children.reason: A reference to a place breaks whenever the place changes. As a specification grows, it is reordered, and its rules may move between the parts of the specification. Since a sid is a node's permanent identifier, moving a node changes its location but never its sid, so no reference by sid breaks.

decisions.problem: The reason said that rules move between domains all the time as a specification grows.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the reason says that rules may move between the parts of the specification, and that a move changes a node's location but never its sid.

decisions.problem: The node did not say whether a node in the archive has a sid too.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the node refers to a node of the specification, since a node in the archive has no sid.

children.title: A rule is made of its text and its reason
children.text:
A rule's text states what the rule requires. Its reason says why that is required. The reason itself requires nothing.

The description of a shortcoming in the technical debt may be an exception: it may carry no reason (§s-2r7k2aeyusgy6fw).
children.reason: Nobody notices that a reason no longer holds while it is buried inside the requirement.

decisions.problem: A rule of the technical debt describes a problem as it stands and states nothing that must hold, which this rule did not admit.
decisions.ruling: Carried from the owner's ruling of the same day on the technical debt (§s-2r7k2aeyusgy6fw): the exception is written here, where the rule it narrows is read.

decisions.problem: The rules call a node's grounds its reason, while the key holding them is rationale, so one thing had two names.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the key becomes reason, renamed with the migration that renames id to location; the key refs stays, a common abbreviation for links that misleads nobody.

decisions.problem: The node was written before the rules of one thought to a sentence (s-juucyammgq4shq8) and of what is applied together (s-6j8ystpj2yzcchq), and before the names of the method were settled.
decisions.ruling: In the owner's name, carrying out those rules and the names the owner settled on 2026-11-07: the wording rewritten, its meaning unchanged.

decisions.problem: The node said that a rule's text states what must hold, which is only one of the things a text does.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the node is about the separate roles of a rule's text and its reason. The text states what the rule requires, and the reason says why that is required.

decisions.problem: The node did not say whether the description of a shortcoming in the technical debt needs a reason.
decisions.ruling: The owner: such a description may be an exception and have no reason, since it states the shortcoming as it is.

children.title: Everything that bears on a node is kept in that node
children.reason: A node is read on its own. What bears on it and is kept elsewhere is missed by whoever reads the node. Kept apart, it also changes unseen.

decisions.problem: The list referred to deferred work as "work put off".
decisions.ruling: The owner: the list says "todos", the name under which a node keeps such work.

children.title: A todo is kept on a node it concerns
children.text:
A todo is deferred work that concerns one node or several. It is kept as an item in the `meta.todos` of a node it concerns. It is never kept in a comment on the node. A todo is removed in each of these cases:
- it is done;
- it is given up.

A todo that concerns several nodes is kept on one of them and cites the others.

An accepted shortcoming in the internal quality of the system's implementation is described in the technical debt (§s-2r7k2aeyusgy6fw), not in a todo.
children.reason: Kept on its node, a todo shows whoever reads the node what work on it is still pending. Kept in a comment, it is missed wherever the todos are collected. Left in place once done or given up, it still shows the work as pending. Kept on one node where it concerns several, it leaves behind no copy that would still show the work as pending.

decisions.problem: The schema held a node's todos, but no rule said that work put off is kept there, nor that it can be listed, while a rule is to hold the work deferred on it.
decisions.ruling: The owner: work put off on one node is kept in its todos, with the day, who its author is and what is to be done, and every item can be listed, the newest first, each with its node.

decisions.problem: The node was written before the rules of one thought to a sentence (s-juucyammgq4shq8) and of what is applied together (s-6j8ystpj2yzcchq), and before the names of the method were settled.
decisions.ruling: In the owner's name, carrying out those rules and the names the owner settled on 2026-11-07: the wording rewritten, its meaning unchanged.

decisions.problem: The node on todos was the only node in its section.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the node moves into the foundations, right after the node on what a node keeps, and its section is removed.

decisions.problem: The node did not say where a todo that concerns several nodes is kept.
decisions.ruling: The owner: such a todo is kept on one of those nodes and cites the others, so that each of them shows an incoming link.

decisions.problem: The reason referred to a node that required a list of all the todos.
decisions.ruling: The owner: that node is deleted, so the reason no longer refers to it. The reason says instead that a todo kept in a comment is missed wherever the todos are collected.

children.title: The single source of truth about the system
children.text:
The specification (§s-qmmzf9nksfsa3qp) is the single source of truth about the system. It defines everything the system is made of: its logic and its structures, such as a set of states, a list of members or a table of routes. The code implements the specification and contains nothing but that implementation.

The checks (§s-m4h279nbaqkpa3t) compare the code with the specification. A rule that leaves its content to be defined by the code is a defect. The rule's owners (§s-6sk8uet75dmq5qz) fix the defect when they revise the rule.

A node of the technical appendix (§s-vj7ercem526zd6v) may name an artifact outside the specification as the place where part of that node's content is kept, such as an interface contract that another team owns. That node names the artifact's version, and the checks compare the code with that version. Adopting a new version of the artifact is a change to the node.
children.reason: Two sources of truth sooner or later disagree, and then nobody knows which of them is right. The code cannot be the source, since code cannot be checked against itself. Content that another team maintains would become a second source if it were copied into the specification, so a node of the technical appendix names that content with its version, and each new version needs the approval of the node's owners.
examples: A service implements a payment interface whose OpenAPI description another team owns. A node of the service's technical appendix names that description and its version 3.2, and the code is checked against version 3.2. The most likely mistake is to write a rule of the base specification that names the description as the rule's content, since the base specification would then depend on a document that changes outside the specification. A project's own guidelines may refine the rule in this node by naming the kinds of external artifacts that the project's technical appendix may name.

decisions.problem: The node was written before the rules of one thought to a sentence (s-juucyammgq4shq8) and of what is applied together (s-6j8ystpj2yzcchq), and before the names of the method were settled.
decisions.ruling: In the owner's name, carrying out those rules and the names the owner settled on 2026-11-07: the wording rewritten, its meaning unchanged.

decisions.problem: The node mixed two rules: the direction in which changes flow, and the single source of truth about the system.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the node states only that the specification, and not the code, is the single source of truth about the system. The direction of change is stated in a node of its own.

decisions.problem: The node did not say whether part of a node's content may be kept in an artifact outside the specification, such as an interface contract that another team owns.
decisions.ruling: The owner: only a node of the technical appendix may name such an artifact, together with its version. The checks compare the code with that version, and adopting a new version is a change to the node.

children.title: Only what the rules require is done
children.text:
Whoever implements the specification, a person or an agent, does only what its rules require. Nothing beyond them is done: no behaviour, no structure and no change that no rule calls for.

This rule does not extend to technical code. Technical code implements none of the system's logic and is required by the technology the system is built with. Examples are a module's re-exports and the glue code a framework needs.
children.reason:
Work beyond the rules is work nobody agreed to. Nothing in the specification checks it. It changes the system without its owners knowing.

Technical code adds nothing to what the system does. It is marked as technical (§s-kgbzk2ph9e6jfb4), so it stays visible.

decisions.problem: A rule binding every store of one kind fitted a store for which it had nothing worth measuring, and a rule saying only that something is not done had been proposed for it.
decisions.ruling: The owner: what no rule requires is understood as not done and needs no rule; an exception refining a general rule is written, for the rule to be exact.

decisions.problem: The node was written before the rules of one thought to a sentence (s-juucyammgq4shq8) and of what is applied together (s-6j8ystpj2yzcchq), and before the names of the method were settled.
decisions.ruling: In the owner's name, carrying out those rules and the names the owner settled on 2026-11-07: the wording rewritten, its meaning unchanged.

decisions.problem: The node mixed the requirement to do only what the rules require with prohibitions and exceptions.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the node says one thing: whoever implements the specification does only what its rules require.

decisions.problem: The node did not say whether the rule extends to technical code, which implements none of the system's logic.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the rule does not extend to technical code, which implements none of the system's logic and is required by the technology the system is built with.

children.title: Approval status
children.text: What the approval status is and who changes it.

children.title: The approval status
children.text:
The approval status can be `draft` or `approved`.

The specification as a whole, a section and a rule each have one.
children.reason: It tells whoever works on the specification what its owners have agreed to and what still awaits their decision.

list.of: the values the approval status can take

decisions.problem: Rules relied on the approval status before any rule said what values it takes and what has one.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a node of its own introduces the approval status and what has one, ahead of the rules that use it.

decisions.problem: The node said that `draft` is the default status, which the schema of the nodes already states.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the rules of the guidelines do not name the default status, which only the schema holds.

children.title: What a draft means
children.text:
The specification, a section or a rule that is not approved at present is a draft:
- While the specification as a whole is a draft, no test has to pass before a change reaches the project's shared branch (§s-m4h279nbaqkpa3t), and the checks give no warning about code that is outside the commit and that no SpecTag binds (§s-kkbqcb9xrpaepwn).
- For a section, the status sums up the state of all the rules inside it. If at least one rule is a draft, the section is a draft too.
- A draft rule is not implemented: no code or test is written or changed for it.
children.reason:
While the specification is a draft, the work is above all on the specification, with the code and the tests secondary.

While the specification or a rule has not yet been approved, it may be incomplete or wrong, so implementing it would either lock its gaps into the code or build the code on guesses.

The status of a section shows at a glance which parts of the specification are in progress and need the rules inside them approved.

Giving sections and nodes a status of their own lets an already largely approved specification be developed and refined without withdrawing its approval.
examples: A rule that has code and tests is reworded and becomes a draft. Its code and tests stay as they are, and the checks accept them. A commit that changes them is refused until an owner approves the new wording. But not: the rule's code and tests have to be removed because the rule has become a draft.

decisions.problem: The node named a node's status checked, the act of agreeing to it a confirmation, and one owner of a part.
decisions.ruling: Carrying out the owner's decision of that day: a node's status is draft or approved, the act is an approval, and a part has owners, one or several.

decisions.problem: The node was written before the rules of one thought to a sentence (s-juucyammgq4shq8) and of what is applied together (s-6j8ystpj2yzcchq), and before the names of the method were settled.
decisions.ruling: In the owner's name, carrying out those rules and the names the owner settled on 2026-11-07: the wording rewritten, its meaning unchanged.

decisions.problem: The node said only that a draft node is not implemented.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the node is replaced by one that says what a draft means for the specification as a whole, for a section and for a rule.

decisions.problem: It was unsettled whether the node should also say that no edit other than a change to a rule's title, text or reason changes the rule's status.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the node says only that a change to a rule's title, text or reason sets the rule to `draft`. It does not add that no other edit changes the status.

decisions.problem: The node mentioned domains, which are defined by an extension of the guidelines that a project may not have chosen.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the rules that every project shares do not name domains. The mention is removed, and the rule's meaning stays the same.

decisions.problem: The node made the check of SpecTags depend on whether the specification as a whole is approved.
decisions.ruling: The owner: while the specification as a whole is a draft, no test has to pass before a change reaches the project's shared branch. Nor do the checks then warn about code that is outside the commit and carries no SpecTag.

decisions.problem: Whether the owner agrees to the recommended option in question 4.1 of the questions about the base specification. Questions 4.1 to 4.6 were shown on one page, each recommended option with the full wording of every node it changes.
decisions.ruling: The owner agreed ("ok", in answer to "Do you agree to the recommended option in all six questions?"): option A in questions 4.1, 4.2 and 4.3, and option B in questions 4.4, 4.5 and 4.6.

decisions.problem: Whether rules 1.3.2, 10.6 and 10.7, which restated rule 9.5 in its earlier wording, change with it.
decisions.ruling: Made without asking, as section 1 of the questions about the base specification says: a technical replacement that carries out the owner's rulings of 2026-11-17 on rows 10.1.26 and 10.1.26a, made together with proposal 2.6, which the owner's answer "but I have already made decisions on these questions" agreed on the owner's behalf.

children.title: When the status is approved
children.text:
The specification, a section and a rule have different conditions for being approved:
- The specification as a whole is approved if an owner has carried out the approval procedure by hand (§s-qzthyh7yqvfhsa2).
- A section is approved while every rule in it is approved (§s-9kfdycuq34beqvs). Nobody approves the section itself.
- A rule is approved while an approval of its current wording is in force (§s-5ah25f6gy99panq).
children.reason: The status `approved` claims that an owner, or an agent on an owner's behalf as the rule on such approvals allows (§s-t5uw8zfxzhfdg86), has agreed to what the status covers. So the status holds only while that agreement holds. A section states no requirement of its own, so an owner has nothing in it to agree to beyond its rules.

decisions.problem: The conditions under which the specification, a section and a rule are approved were stated in three separate rules.
decisions.ruling: The owner: one node states everything about when the status is `approved`.

decisions.problem: The reason said that the status `approved` states that one of the rule's owners has agreed, although an agent may now approve a node on an owner's behalf.
decisions.ruling: The owner accepted that the status claims the rule's present wording was approved by one of its owners or, as "What an agent approves on an owner's behalf" (s-t5uw8zfxzhfdg86) allows, by an agent on an owner's behalf.

decisions.problem: Whether the owner agrees to proposal 2.7 of the questions about the base specification. Proposals 2.1 to 2.9, each of which carries out a decision the owner had already made, were shown on one page with each node in full.
decisions.ruling: The owner answered "but I have already made decisions on these questions": the proposal only carries out the item from group 6 (2026-11-24) under which an approval "is in force" rather than "stands", so it is agreed to on the owner's behalf.

children.title: Only a node's owners approve it
children.text:
A node is approved by at least one of its owners, or on an owner's behalf as §s-t5uw8zfxzhfdg86 allows, and by nobody else. An approval names whoever gave it.

An owner of a `TableRule` may approve the whole table at once. Doing so approves every node in its cells that is a draft, and each of those approvals names that owner.
children.reason: An approval means that someone accountable for a rule has agreed to what it states or, in the cases that §s-t5uw8zfxzhfdg86 lists, that an agent has approved the rule on that person's behalf and reported it to them. So it is theirs to give. A named approver is checked against the node's owners. A named approver can also be asked about the approval later. The requirements in a table are read and agreed to together, so approving them one by one would only repeat a single agreement.
examples: A project's own guidelines may require a node to be approved by two of its owners, which is what a team in a regulated industry needs.

decisions.problem: One owner confirmed every node, which binds a growing specification to one person, and the confirmations were kept outside the specification, where nobody else could check them.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a domain may name its owners in its header; a confirmation names who gave it, beside the fingerprint of the wording, is kept with the specification and is accepted only under that owner's signature. A confirmation read off the approvals of a merge request was declined, since it would tie what a status means to one hosting platform.

decisions.problem: Owners could be named on a domain's header alone, and a confirmation was to carry its owner's signature, made with a key no agent can use.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the specification has one owner, and a domain or a section may have its own, taken as a task is taken, oneself included; a confirmation names its owner and carries no signature, the agent's hooks guarding the status.

decisions.problem: The spec-review skill had the agent confirm, unshown, a node changed only to state what its owner had confirmed in another node, or by a replacement changing no meaning, while this rule let nobody but the owner confirm a node.
decisions.ruling: The owner: such a node is confirmed in its owner's name by the agent that made the change for that owner, which reports the confirmation to the owner; the owner may withdraw it. The owner amended the principle that nothing unconfirmed is implemented to the same effect.

decisions.problem: A part could name only one owner, while a team shares the reading of a part.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a part may have several owners with equal rights, any of whom approves; the approval names who gave it.

decisions.problem: The node was written before the rules of one thought to a sentence (s-juucyammgq4shq8) and of what is applied together (s-6j8ystpj2yzcchq), and before the names of the method were settled.
decisions.ruling: In the owner's name, carrying out those rules and the names the owner settled on 2026-11-07: the wording rewritten, its meaning unchanged.

decisions.problem: The node did not say whether an owner of a `TableRule` must approve each node in its cells separately.
decisions.ruling: The owner: an owner of a `TableRule` may approve the whole table at once. Doing so approves every draft node in its cells, and each of those approvals names that owner.

decisions.problem: The node did not say how many of a node's owners must approve it.
decisions.ruling: The owner: an approval by at least one of a node's owners is enough. The example shows a project's own guidelines requiring two approvals.

decisions.problem: The reason said that an approval means an owner's agreement, which does not hold where an agent approves a node on an owner's behalf.
decisions.ruling: The owner: an approval means that someone accountable for the rule has agreed to it. In the cases where an agent may approve on an owner's behalf, it means that the agent has approved the rule and reported it to that owner.

children.title: What an approval covers
children.reason: A node requires only what its wording states. Its kind is part of that wording, since the kind decides, for example, whether code must implement the node. So an approval lapses when that wording changes, and not otherwise. Everything else about a node changes as the specification grows around it.

decisions.problem: A data record node holds its fields apart from its text (s-e877bnfa559tvk9), and a field changed would have left the status standing over a structure the owner never confirmed.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a data record node's fields are part of the wording a confirmation covers.

decisions.problem: A kind of node came to carry values beside its text, and a value changed would have left the status standing over values the owner never confirmed.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the values a node's kind carries beside its text are part of the wording a confirmation covers, as a data record node's fields are.

decisions.problem: One person confirmed every node, and the values a confirmation covered were listed by the kinds of node one project uses.
decisions.ruling: The owner: an owner of the part a node stands in confirms it (§s-67vekyup7y8smap), and a confirmation covers whatever values the node's kind carries beside its text. An owner's own change to a wording needs a new confirmation as anyone else's does, since the fingerprint of the wording, not who changed it, decides.

decisions.problem: A move was said to leave the status as it is, while only a node's owner confirms it, so a node moved under another owner stood checked over words that owner never read.
decisions.ruling: The owner: checked means the node's owner confirmed its present wording; a move or a change that gives the node another owner empties its status.

decisions.problem: The reason held that a checked status claims its owner read the words a node holds, while a node may now be confirmed in its owner's name where its change states nothing new.
decisions.ruling: In line with the owner's ruling on §s-67vekyup7y8smap: a checked status claims the owner agreed to what the node states.

decisions.problem: No rule said who may withdraw a confirmation, while the procedure let anyone.
decisions.ruling: The owner: anyone may withdraw a confirmation, and the withdrawal names whoever made it; the SpecSheriff guidelines a project takes stay as they were confirmed where they are written (§s-bsya3febm6u64ab).

decisions.problem: What is built into a node from other nodes, a domain's header's index of sections, was left out of the wording a confirmation covers by the tools alone, and the values gathered beside a field were to be built so too.
decisions.ruling: In line with the owner's ruling on s-ju5vcanbjph7mgh: a change to what is built into a node from other nodes leaves its status as it is.

decisions.problem: The node named a kind of node "data record" and a node's place "address" or "id".
decisions.ruling: A technical replacement following the owner's decisions of that day: a data record is a RecordType, and a node's address or id is its location.

decisions.problem: Checked was read three ways once the specification and its domains had a status too: a node's wording confirmed by its owner, every node of a section or a domain confirmed, and a specification put live. A move or a change of owner emptied a node's status, while such a change is most often technical.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a node's status is draft or approved, a section's and a domain's header's built from what they hold; whether someone may approve is settled when the approval is given, so a change of owners or a move keeps it.

decisions.problem: The node was written before the rules of one thought to a sentence (s-juucyammgq4shq8) and of what is applied together (s-6j8ystpj2yzcchq), and before the names of the method were settled.
decisions.ruling: In the owner's name, carrying out those rules and the names the owner settled on 2026-11-07: the wording rewritten, its meaning unchanged.

decisions.problem: The rules on approval were split between the foundations and another section.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the node moves into the subsection on approval within the foundations, and the section that held it is removed.

decisions.problem: The node did not say whether an approval covers a node's examples.
decisions.ruling: The owner: an approval covers the examples too, so a change to a node's examples makes the node a draft.

decisions.problem: The node did not say what the wording of a node in a cell of a `TableRule` includes.
decisions.ruling: The owner: that wording also includes the text cells of the node's row and the headings of its column and of its group.

decisions.problem: Whether the owner agrees to the recommended option in question 4.1 of the questions about the base specification. Questions 4.1 to 4.6 were shown on one page, each recommended option with the full wording of every node it changes.
decisions.ruling: The owner agreed ("ok", in answer to "Do you agree to the recommended option in all six questions?"): option A in questions 4.1, 4.2 and 4.3, and option B in questions 4.4, 4.5 and 4.6.

skills/tools/test/unit/reindex.test.ts::@spec s-5ah25f6gy99panq makes a draft an approved node no approval stands for, sections and headers left out, and names each

children.title: What an agent approves on an owner's behalf
children.reason: An owner's approval is worth waiting for only where a wording states something new that nothing else checks. A wording that restates an approved one, or does not change the meaning, states nothing new. What a node of the technical appendix adds to the rule it implements is checked by the independent reviewer in the commit in which the node is approved (§s-nyh9yk22ba6g77q). The agent's report informs the owner of each such approval, so that the owner can withdraw an approval they disagree with (§s-fpq35tf3pehgk64).
examples: While implementing an approved rule stating that an idle session expires, the agent adds a node of the technical appendix that sets the idle limit at 30 minutes and has an `implements` link to that rule. The agent approves the node on the owner's behalf and reports it. But not: a node that the agent adds to the section on the stack, which implements no rule, is approved by the agent in the same way.

decisions.problem: Whether each node an agent adds to the technical appendix while implementing must wait for an owner's approval before its code can be committed.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the agent approves such nodes on the owner's behalf and reports them to the owner, and the principle "Nothing unapproved is implemented" is changed to say so.

decisions.problem: Which nodes of the technical appendix the agent may approve on the owner's behalf, given that an approval records only the git identity it was made under.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the boundary is set by the node itself, so that the tools can check it: a node of the technical appendix with an `implements` link to an approved rule of the base specification. The independent reviewer judges every such node whose approval a commit contains, whoever approved it. The rules of the base specification, and the nodes that have no such link, are approved only by an owner.

decisions.problem: The rules on approval were split between the foundations and another section.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the node moves into the subsection on approval within the foundations, and the section that held it is removed.

decisions.problem: The node did not say whether an agent may approve a node on an owner's behalf in a case other than those it lists.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the list of cases is exhaustive.

children.title: Who may withdraw a node's approval
children.text: Anyone may withdraw the approval of a node, except the approval of a node of the SpecSheriff guidelines that a project uses (§s-bsya3febm6u64ab) or of an extension that the project has chosen (§s-9ttvcwpqkehm58g). A withdrawal makes the node a draft. The withdrawal names whoever made it.
children.reason: A withdrawal approves nothing on anyone's behalf, so whoever finds an approved rule wrong can stop any further change to its code (§s-utvqbypzhmgndug) without waiting for its owners. The name on it tells the owners whom to ask. The SpecSheriff guidelines and their extensions are approved where they are written (§s-bsya3febm6u64ab), so not just anyone may withdraw their approval.

decisions.problem: The rules on approval were split between the foundations and another section.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the node moves into the subsection on approval within the foundations, and the section that held it is removed.

decisions.problem: The node exempted from the withdrawal of approval a rule of a project's own guidelines that states that the specification is approved.
decisions.ruling: The owner: that exception is removed, together with the sentence in the reason that explained it.

decisions.problem: The node did not say whether anyone may withdraw the approval of a node of an extension that the project has chosen.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the exception for the nodes of the SpecSheriff guidelines also covers the nodes of an extension that the project has chosen. The owner chose to state this in each rule it concerns, rather than in one general rule.

children.title: How a section's approval status is determined
children.text: The SpecSheriff tools derive a section's approval status from every node under it other than a section, at any depth. They recompute it after every change to the specification. Nobody sets it by hand.
children.reason: A section's status lets one easily see the approval state of the nodes inside it. This can be useful where only sections are visible.

decisions.problem: A section and a domain's header were confirmed as a rule is, so their status claimed an agreement to words that require nothing, and said nothing of the nodes they hold.
decisions.ruling: The owner: their status is the state of what they hold, built and only shown, whatever the number of rules; their own wording is meta-information nobody approves.

decisions.problem: The node was written before the rules of one thought to a sentence (s-juucyammgq4shq8) and of what is applied together (s-6j8ystpj2yzcchq), and before the names of the method were settled.
decisions.ruling: In the owner's name, carrying out those rules and the names the owner settled on 2026-11-07: the wording rewritten, its meaning unchanged.

decisions.problem: The rules on approval were split between the foundations and another section.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the node moves into the subsection on approval within the foundations, and the section that held it is removed.

decisions.problem: A reviewer had cut the reason down to saying that a section's status is derived from its nodes. Why a section has a status at all was lost.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the reason says that a section's status shows at a glance the approval status of the nodes inside it, which helps where only sections are visible.
