children.title: The test
children.text: What the implementation of a rule starts with.

children.title: The test comes before the code
children.text: When a rule is implemented, its test is written first. The code that implements the rule is written second, to pass that test.
children.reason: A test written first tests the rule, not whatever the code happened to do.

decisions.problem: Two tests added with a feature opened with no sid, and nothing checked that a test of the system's code names the rule it verifies.
decisions.ruling: The owner: tags and tests that cite the specification are the general rule for all code, checked at every commit.

decisions.problem: Tests of what a term of contracts defines opened with the term's sid, which the rule as worded refused.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a test opens with the sid of the checked rule or term it verifies.

decisions.problem: A test whose change only moved a citation onto a sid was held to open its name with the sid of a checked rule it verifies, which a test of a rule not yet checked cannot do, while a declaration changed only so owed no tag.
decisions.ruling: The owner agreed that a change to a test that only rewrites its citations or its comments owes it no such name, as §s-kgbzk2ph9e6jfb4 already holds for a declaration.

decisions.problem: A test bound to its rule by the opening of its name cannot be written in a language whose names cannot hold a hyphen.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a test declares the sid of what it verifies in the way its framework names a test (§s-rwqzepmrt77rv35).

decisions.problem: The rule let a test whose change only rewrote its citations or comments go without a sid, an exemption for tests written before tests carried sids, and it was worded for a reader who already knew the procedure.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a test always carries the sid of what it verifies; the rule is worded as the procedure it is — the test first, the code second, the test carrying the rule's sid and the code its tag.

decisions.problem: A test could carry the sid of a node of a kind a project's own guidelines bind to tests, while the schema every project reads admits only the kinds it defines and nothing lets a project declare another; and the check accepted a test carrying the sid of any node, a section's included.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the kinds of node are those the schema defines, the same in every project; a test carries the sid of a rule or a term.

decisions.problem: The reason called a rule with no test implemented, while a rule is implemented only with a passing test carrying its sid.
decisions.ruling: In line with the owner's ruling on §s-6fw72j65jkqrfpf: a rule whose code has no test is carried out on trust.

decisions.problem: A test could carry the sid of a rule or a term only, while a node of a project's own kind is implemented as a rule is; and only a data record's code was said to owe no test, while any code generated from a node is held to what the node produces.
decisions.ruling: In line with the owner's ruling on §s-vsh384ybt4w25a2: a test may carry the sid of a node of a project's own kind; code written for a node owes a test, code generated from it owes none.

decisions.problem: The node named a kind of node "data record" and a node's place "address" or "id".
decisions.ruling: A technical replacement following the owner's decisions of that day: a data record is a RecordType, and a node's address or id is its location.

decisions.problem: The node called the mark binding a symbol to the node it implements a tag.
decisions.ruling: A technical replacement following the owner's decision of that day: a tag is called SpecTag.

decisions.problem: A test carried its rule's sid bare, in its name or a mark, while the code carried a SpecTag; and rewriting the one into the other would have counted as changing every test.
decisions.ruling: In line with the owner's ruling on §s-rwqzepmrt77rv35: the test carries the SpecTag, and a rewrite naming the same node changes no test, as moving a citation changes no code (§s-kgbzk2ph9e6jfb4).

decisions.problem: The node named a node's status checked, the act of agreeing to it a confirmation, and one owner of a part.
decisions.ruling: Carrying out the owner's decision of that day: a node's status is draft or approved, the act is an approval, and a part has owners, one or several.

decisions.problem: The node was written before the rules of one thought to a sentence (s-juucyammgq4shq8) and of what is applied together (s-6j8ystpj2yzcchq), and before the names of the method were settled.
decisions.ruling: In the owner's name, carrying out those rules and the names the owner settled on 2026-11-07: the wording rewritten, its meaning unchanged.

decisions.problem: The node on writing a rule's test before its code also required a test to refer to its rule.
decisions.ruling: The owner: that requirement moves to a node of its own.

children.title: A test's reference to its rule
children.text: A test must contain a reference to a rule of the specification.
children.reason: A test without a reference to its rule tests something nobody can name. A test names a rule's behaviour, which survives refactoring that moves and renames the code underneath it. So a test's reference to its rule is stable.

decisions.problem: The requirement that a test refers to its rule stood in the node on writing the test before the code.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a node of its own states that a test must contain a reference to a rule of the specification.

children.title: The code
children.text: How the code follows the rule.

children.title: Code changes only as a result of a change to the specification
children.text:
The code's behaviour changes only as a result of a change to the specification, not by editing the code directly. The process is always one-way: rule, test, code.

A defect or an edge case is no exception to this order: the code is not changed first.
children.reason: The one-way approach keeps the code in agreement with the specification and ensures that there is always a single source of truth.

decisions.problem: The second paragraph said more than that defects and edge cases are no exception to the order.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the paragraph says only that a defect or an edge case is no exception to the order, so the code is not changed first. That a defect in a rule is fixed in the rule first goes without saying.

children.title: How code is bound to its rules
children.reason: Binding each file of the system's code as precisely as its format allows lets the checks immediately find code that has lost its link to the specification.
examples: A stylesheet whose symbols the checks cannot identify has its SpecTag in a comment at its start.
A JSON file that holds the texts a user interface shows has an entry in the bindings file. The entry names the JSON file and holds its SpecTags.

A Python file defines a function and ends with a call, outside every function, that starts a server. A comment at the start of the file holds the SpecTag of the rule that the call implements. The most likely mistake is to leave the call unbound because the file's symbols carry SpecTags.

decisions.problem: One tag per changed file was owed, and only in a domain with a checked rule of its own, so code implementing two checked rules of another domain shipped with no tag, and logic no rule stated passed beside it.
decisions.ruling: The owner: code changes only through the specification and never the reverse, enforced by scripts that refuse logic without a reference back to the specification and by an independent reviewer; every declaration a commit adds or changes carries a tag, in every domain and in contracts.

decisions.problem: A tag was owed only by a declaration a commit added or changed, so code nobody had touched since the rules were written stayed untagged, and whether a rule asked for it could not be seen.
decisions.ruling: The owner: every declaration always carries a tag; a project adopting the method tags its code before the check is turned on.

decisions.problem: The ruling of 2026-10-27 had a project adopting the method tag its code before the check is turned on, and nothing said when the check is turned on.
decisions.ruling: In line with the owner's ruling on §s-qzthyh7yqvfhsa2: the check refuses every symbol without a SpecTag from the commit putting the specification live.

decisions.problem: The rule exempted every test from tags by where it lives, and said a test carries the sid of what it verifies.
decisions.ruling: The owner: every symbol of the system's code but its tests carries a tag; a test carries the sid of the node it is written from, since it is written from the node's logic and verifies the code written for it.

decisions.problem: The node called the mark binding a symbol to the node it implements a tag.
decisions.ruling: A technical replacement following the owner's decision of that day: a tag is called SpecTag.

decisions.problem: The node named a test's reference to its node a sid, or read a SpecTag as standing only on a symbol, once a test came to carry a SpecTag too.
decisions.ruling: A technical replacement in line with the owner's rulings of the same day on a test's SpecTag and on a draft: a test names its node by its SpecTag, and the check that binds symbols to their nodes reads only the symbols of code other than tests.

decisions.problem: The node named a node's status checked, the act of agreeing to it a confirmation, and one owner of a part.
decisions.ruling: Carrying out the owner's decision of that day: a node's status is draft or approved, the act is an approval, and a part has owners, one or several.

decisions.problem: The node was written before the rules of one thought to a sentence (s-juucyammgq4shq8) and of what is applied together (s-6j8ystpj2yzcchq), and before the names of the method were settled.
decisions.ruling: In the owner's name, carrying out those rules and the names the owner settled on 2026-11-07: the wording rewritten, its meaning unchanged.

decisions.problem: The node on how code is bound to its rules also covered how tests are bound.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the node covers code only. The paragraph on tests and its reason move to the node on a test's reference to its rule.

decisions.problem: The node bound code to its rules only by a SpecTag before each symbol, which a file without identifiable symbols or without comments cannot carry.
decisions.ruling: The owner: code is bound by a SpecTag before each symbol, by SpecTags at the start of its file, or by an entry in a bindings file at the root of the repository. The formats that allow no comments are JSON and those that a project's own guidelines name.

decisions.problem: Whether the owner agrees to group 3 of stage 2 of task T25, items 27 to 32 and the owner's ruling of 2026-11-24 on comments and whitespace, shown on one page with each node in full.
decisions.ruling: The owner agreed to the group ("ok", in answer to "Do you agree to group 3?").

decisions.problem: Whether the owner agrees to proposal 2.8 of the questions about the base specification. Proposals 2.1 to 2.9, each of which carries out a decision the owner had already made, were shown on one page with each node in full.
decisions.ruling: The owner answered "but I have already made decisions on these questions": the proposal only carries out the owner's rulings of 2026-11-17 on rows 10.1.26 and 10.1.26a, so it is agreed to on the owner's behalf.

decisions.problem: Whether the owner agrees to the recommended option in question 4.3 of the questions about the base specification. Questions 4.1 to 4.6 were shown on one page, each recommended option with the full wording of every node it changes.
decisions.ruling: The owner agreed ("ok", in answer to "Do you agree to the recommended option in all six questions?"): option A in questions 4.1, 4.2 and 4.3, and option B in questions 4.4, 4.5 and 4.6.

children.title: The checks
children.text: What holds together the whole path from a node to the code.

children.title: What the checks enforce
children.text:
The following are checked mechanically:
- that the specification conforms to the rules of the guidelines that the main table of checks (§s-jau82aq9juv9zzh), or the table of checks of an extension (§s-gpzs5fcxvp6jkrp), lists;
- that the specification and the code still agree with each other.

Every check except the review (§s-m4h279nbaqkpa3t) is deterministic.

A failed check refuses the change, unless the table that lists the check says otherwise (§s-jau82aq9juv9zzh).
children.reason: Every check but the review is binary, so a refusal requires nobody's judgement. A check that sometimes refuses for a reason nobody can reproduce is bypassed at the first opportunity and never trusted again.

decisions.problem: Whether the owner agrees to group 3 of stage 2 of task T25, items 27 to 32 and the owner's ruling of 2026-11-24 on comments and whitespace, shown on one page with each node in full.
decisions.ruling: The owner agreed to the group ("ok", in answer to "Do you agree to group 3?").

children.title: What the independent reviewer judges
children.reason: No script can decide whether code does only what its rules say, whether a comment agrees with the code and its rules, whether a rule's implementation really needs no change, or whether a node of the technical appendix agrees with the base specification. So these judgements are made by an independent reviewer. Code generated from the specification only restates the specification, so the reviewer has nothing to judge there.

decisions.problem: Who verifies a commit message's statement that a rule's implementation needs no change.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the independent reviewer verifies it, and the principle on deterministic checks is extended to say so.

decisions.problem: Who checks a node of the technical appendix that an agent approved on an owner's behalf.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the independent reviewer checks it, in the commit in which the node is approved, whoever approved it.

decisions.problem: The node said that the checks keep the specification "holding together on its own". It did not say which rules are checked, that the checks run after each of an agent's edits, or what a failed check does.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the checks ensure that the specification conforms to the rules of the guidelines that the table of checks lists. They also run after each edit an agent makes, and a failed check refuses the change unless the table says otherwise.

decisions.problem: The node did not say when the tests must pass or where they run.
decisions.ruling: The owner: while the specification is approved, the tests must pass before a change reaches the project's shared branch. The project's own guidelines name where the tests run, and while the specification is a draft, no test has to pass.

decisions.problem: The node did not require the tests of a project's own generators to pass.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the tests of a project's own generators must pass too, like those of the system's code and of the project's own checks.

decisions.problem: The node named only the main table of checks, although an extension may have a table of checks of its own.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the node also names the table of checks of an extension, which refines the main table of checks.

decisions.problem: The node did not say which approved nodes of the technical appendix the reviewer judges, or what the reviewer judges them on.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the reviewer judges an approved node of the technical appendix only if it has an `implements` link to a rule of the base specification. The reviewer judges whether the node refines the rules it implements and contradicts no rule of the base specification.

decisions.problem: The reason cited the current rule on the tests on a push while the specification is a draft (s-xhcmchcngykvn2k) for why no test has to pass while the specification is a draft. The new form drops that rule.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the reason states the ground itself. While the specification is a draft, the work is focused on the specification itself, so no test has to pass.

decisions.problem: Whether the owner agrees to group 3 of stage 2 of task T25, items 27 to 32 and the owner's ruling of 2026-11-24 on comments and whitespace, shown on one page with each node in full.
decisions.ruling: The owner agreed to the group ("ok", in answer to "Do you agree to group 3?").

children.title: When the tests must pass
children.text: As long as the specification has the status `approved`, the tests of the system's code (§s-hheus6f395ynqvc) and of a project's own checks (§s-2fau85dfyyeq66m) and generators (§s-km4x4s26kv7pjze) must pass before a change reaches the project's shared branch. The project's own guidelines (§s-u7tw6m8npxmv5tu) name where the tests run, such as on every push or on a shared server before a merge.
children.reason: The tests are not run on a commit, since a test suite takes longer than anyone should wait for a commit. A change not yet shared misleads nobody, so its tests can wait until it is shared. Where they run is the project's choice, since some suites take hours or need what a developer's machine lacks. While the specification is a draft, the work is focused on the specification itself, so no test has to pass.
examples: A project whose tests need a database states in its own guidelines that the tests run on a shared server before a merge. A push from a developer's machine then runs no tests, and the merge waits until the tests pass.

decisions.problem: Whether the owner agrees to group 3 of stage 2 of task T25, items 27 to 32 and the owner's ruling of 2026-11-24 on comments and whitespace, shown on one page with each node in full.
decisions.ruling: The owner agreed to the group ("ok", in answer to "Do you agree to group 3?").

children.title: Extensions of the guidelines
children.text: What holds for any extension of the guidelines, and why any combination of extensions works.

children.title: What an extension of the guidelines is
children.text:
An extension of the guidelines is a named set of rules beyond the SpecSheriff guidelines, which every project shares. Its rules are not rules of the SpecSheriff guidelines. It is delivered with the SpecSheriff plugin, together with the SpecSheriff tools that carry out its rules.

A project uses an extension only if it chooses to.
children.reason: Not every system needs every rule. Rules a project does not use only add to what its agent has to read, so they are kept apart from the rules every project shares, and each extension is kept apart from the others. The rules of an extension are carried out by tools, so the two are delivered together.

decisions.problem: Rules that not every system needs were part of the guidelines that every project shares.
decisions.ruling: The owner: such rules form extensions of the guidelines, which are delivered with the SpecSheriff plugin and the tools that carry them out. A project uses an extension only if it chooses to.

decisions.problem: The node did not say whether the rules of an extension are rules of the SpecSheriff guidelines, or whether the extensions are kept together.
decisions.ruling: The owner accepted that the rules of an extension are not rules of the SpecSheriff guidelines. Each extension is kept apart from the others.

decisions.problem: Nothing in the guidelines said how the extensions are kept apart in the files of the guidelines.
decisions.ruling: The owner left this to the agent, which decided that each extension is kept in a file of its own.

children.title: How an extension relates to the rules of the guidelines
children.text: A rule of an extension of the guidelines (§s-mbmnsnxenmavu3z) either adds a rule beyond the SpecSheriff guidelines (§s-u7tw6m8npxmv5tu) or refines one of their rules (§s-sn6au3vcr9uy5pm). It is consistent with every rule of the SpecSheriff guidelines.
children.reason: A rule of the SpecSheriff guidelines then holds in every project that uses the SpecSheriff guidelines, whatever extensions the project has chosen. A project's own guidelines likewise only refine the rules that they build on, or add rules to them (§s-u7tw6m8npxmv5tu), so a reader, an agent or a tool can rely on a rule of the SpecSheriff guidelines without reading the extensions a project uses.
examples: An extension that divides the base specification into parts refines the rule on links: a link may cross the boundary of a part. The most likely mistake is an extension that says that a check of the guidelines does not run in a project that uses that extension.

decisions.problem: Under the owner's ruling of 2026-11-11, an extension could change a rule of the SpecSheriff guidelines through an `overrides` link, so a rule of the guidelines might not hold in every project.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a rule of an extension only adds a rule or refines a rule of the SpecSheriff guidelines, and it is consistent with every rule of the guidelines. An extension no longer changes a rule of the guidelines, so the `overrides` link is withdrawn.

children.title: A rule of the SpecSheriff guidelines names no particular extension
children.text: The text and the reason of a rule of the SpecSheriff guidelines name no particular extension and cite none of its nodes. Such a rule declares no link to a node of an extension.
children.reason: An extension may disappear or be a draft, so a rule depending on it would then be wrong.

decisions.problem: A rule of the SpecSheriff guidelines could rely on an extension that a project has not chosen.
decisions.ruling: The owner decided that the rules not every project needs belong in extensions of the guidelines. So a rule of the SpecSheriff guidelines names no particular extension, cites none of its nodes and declares no link to them.

children.title: Independence of extensions
children.reason: A project chooses each extension of the guidelines separately (§s-mbmnsnxenmavu3z). An extension that does not rely on another extension can then be used alone or together with any other extension.
examples: A rule of an extension about data formats says that a format is declared in the section of the base specification that describes where the data of that format first appear. In a project that also divides its base specification into domains, that section is in a domain, and the rule does not need to mention domains. The most likely mistake in that case: the rule says that a format is declared in the domain where its data first appear.

decisions.problem: An earlier draft let an extension rely on another extension, keeping the rules that relied on it in a section of their own.
decisions.ruling: The owner: each extension relies only on the SpecSheriff guidelines and names no other extension, so any combination of extensions works. The earlier draft is withdrawn.

decisions.problem: The rule limited the words that a rule of an extension uses and the nodes that it cites, but not the types of the links it declares.
decisions.ruling: The owner accepted the reviewer's proposal: the links that such a rule declares are only of the types that the guidelines or its own extension define.

children.title: Configuring extensions
children.text: An owner of the specification chooses which extensions of the guidelines (§s-mbmnsnxenmavu3z) the project uses. The owner does so personally, using a utility from the SpecSheriff plugin, or through an agent working for that owner. The choice is recorded in the repository's configuration. An agent changes the choice only when that owner asks it to.
children.reason: Choosing an extension changes the rules that bind everyone working on the project. Therefore the choice is made by those accountable for the specification, just as approving the specification is (§s-qzthyh7yqvfhsa2). Because the choice is recorded in the repository, it is the same in every clone.
examples: An owner opens the utility, sees every extension that the installed plugin delivers, and marks one of them as chosen. Later the owner asks the agent in the chat to enable another one, and the agent does so on the owner's behalf. The most likely mistake is an agent that enables an extension that it takes to be needed for the work at hand, although the owner did not ask for it.

decisions.problem: Nothing in the guidelines said where a project records which extensions of the guidelines it uses.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the extensions that a project has chosen are recorded in its configuration in the repository. Only the chosen ones are recorded, since the available ones come with each release of the plugin.

decisions.problem: Nothing in the guidelines said who chooses the extensions that a project uses, or how.
decisions.ruling: The owner: an owner of the specification chooses them, either personally, using a utility from the SpecSheriff plugin, or through an agent working for that owner. An agent changes the choice only when that owner asks it to.

children.title: An extension that a node depends on stays chosen
children.text:
An extension of the guidelines (§s-mbmnsnxenmavu3z) that the project has chosen (§s-9ttvcwpqkehm58g) stays chosen while a node of the specification that is not part of the extension depends on it. A node depends on the extension while it does any of the following:
- is of a kind that the extension adds, or holds a property or a link of a type that the extension adds;
- links to one of the extension's nodes.

The procedure that withdraws the choice of an extension refuses to withdraw it while a node depends on the extension. The refusal names each node that depends on the extension.
children.reason: Withdrawing the choice of an extension that a node still depends on would leave that node relying on rules and definitions that no longer hold in the project.
examples: An owner asks to withdraw the choice of an extension while the specification still holds nodes of a kind that the extension adds. The procedure refuses to withdraw the choice and names those nodes by their sids. Once the nodes are removed, the choice of the extension can be withdrawn. The most likely mistake is a procedure that withdraws the choice and leaves it to the checks to refuse the next commit.

decisions.problem: Withdrawing the choice of an extension could leave nodes that rely on what the extension defines.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a chosen extension stays chosen while a node of the specification that is not part of the extension depends on it. The procedure that withdraws the choice refuses to do so while such a node exists, naming each such node.

children.title: The table of checks of an extension
children.text: An extension of the guidelines (§s-mbmnsnxenmavu3z) that adds checks lists all of them in its table of checks, one `TableRule` (§s-5fewsp22mmdz7y6) of its own. The table of checks of an extension refines the main table of checks (§s-jau82aq9juv9zzh). It has the same columns as the main table of checks.
children.reason: The main table of checks names no particular extension (§s-chk5hnzmcpeqj25), so the checks of an extension cannot be listed in it. In one table, every check of an extension can be seen at a glance, together with what its failure costs.
examples: An extension that divides the base specification into parts has a check that every part has a header. It lists that check in the table of checks of the extension, not in the main table of checks. The most likely mistake is a row in the main table of checks that applies only where a project has chosen that extension.

decisions.problem: Where an extension of the guidelines keeps its checks, since the table of checks names no particular extension.
decisions.ruling: The owner: each extension keeps its checks in one rule of its own, a table with the same columns as the table of checks, which refines it.

decisions.problem: Once each extension had a table of checks of its own, the name "the table of checks" no longer told the tables apart.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the table of the SpecSheriff guidelines is "the main table of checks", and the table of an extension is "the table of checks of an extension". This node introduces the second name.

children.title: The parts of the specification
children.text: The parts that the specification consists of.

children.title: The guidelines and the appendix of the tools
children.reason: The tools can change while the rules they carry out stay the same, so the appendix of the tools is kept apart from the rules. The guidelines hardly change, while the appendix of the tools changes with every release of the tools, as a technical appendix does.

decisions.problem: The guidelines named the commands, the hooks, the files and the parser of the tools that check them, which their own rule forbids a base specification to do.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the guidelines apply the split between base and appendix to themselves, so that another toolset can implement the same base.

decisions.problem: The node was written before the rules of one thought to a sentence (s-juucyammgq4shq8) and of what is applied together (s-6j8ystpj2yzcchq), and before the names of the method were settled.
decisions.ruling: In the owner's name, carrying out those rules and the names the owner settled on 2026-11-07: the wording rewritten, its meaning unchanged.

decisions.problem: The node divided the guidelines into "their base" and the appendix of the tools, mirroring the division of the specification.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the node refers simply to the guidelines, and the paragraph that introduced the name "the base of the guidelines" is removed.

decisions.problem: The node said that the guidelines name no technology, applying to them the ban meant for a project's base specification.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the ban on naming a technology applies only to a project's base specification, not to the guidelines. The sentence stating the ban is removed from this node.

decisions.problem: The node did not settle whether the appendix of the tools is part of the guidelines.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the appendix of the tools is a separate document and not part of the guidelines. What is checked, when, and what a failure costs stay in the rules of the guidelines.

children.title: The appendix of the tools implements the guidelines
children.text: The appendix of the tools never contradicts the rules of the guidelines it implements. Each rule of the appendix links to at least one of those rules.
children.reason: Kept in separate documents, the appendix of the tools and the rules it implements can drift apart unnoticed. Bound to the rule it implements, a rule of the appendix is found when that rule changes.

decisions.problem: The node did not say how the appendix of the tools relates to the rules of the guidelines.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the appendix of the tools never contradicts the rules of the guidelines it implements. Each of its rules links to at least one of those rules.

children.title: A project's own guidelines
children.reason:
The SpecSheriff guidelines, shared by every project, let a tool, a skill or a reader move from one project to the next. A project may also need what they cannot foresee.

A project's own rules refine or extend the rules they build on, and never contradict them, as the technical appendix does with the base. A rule of the SpecSheriff guidelines or of an extension can then be relied on in every project that uses it, without reading that project's own rules.

decisions.problem: The node read as though every project must write rules of its own, and it said that a project's own rule implements the rule it builds on.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a project may add rules of its own where it needs them, but it need not. A project's own rule extends the rule it builds on, rather than implementing it.

decisions.problem: The node mentioned domains, which are defined by an extension of the guidelines that a project may not have chosen.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the rules that every project shares do not name domains. The mention is removed, and the rule's meaning stays the same.

decisions.problem: The item on the SpecSheriff guidelines counted the appendix of the tools as part of them, and the list did not name the extensions a project has chosen.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the appendix of the tools is not part of a project's guidelines, and the chosen extensions form an item of their own. A project's own rules may also refine a rule of a chosen extension.

children.title: The minimum the shared rules require
children.text: A rule of the SpecSheriff guidelines (§s-u7tw6m8npxmv5tu), or of an extension of the guidelines (§s-mbmnsnxenmavu3z), requires only a minimum. That minimum is what every project that uses the rule must do for the rule to serve the purpose stated in its reason. Where a value may differ between projects, such as who owns the specification, only a project's own guidelines name that value or any default for it.
children.reason: A project's own guidelines only refine or extend a rule they build on (§s-u7tw6m8npxmv5tu). Replacing a default that such a rule sets would change the rule too. So every requirement and every value in such a rule binds each project that uses the rule, even a project that does not need that requirement or cannot meet it.
examples: A rule requires that a node be approved by at least one of its owners. A project's own guidelines may require two approvals. The most likely mistake is a rule that requires two approvals, since a project with a single owner cannot meet that rule.

decisions.problem: It was unsettled whether a rule shared by every project may require more than every project needs.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a shared rule requires only the minimum that every project needs for the rule to serve its purpose. A project's own guidelines only tighten or refine it.

children.title: How a project uses the SpecSheriff guidelines and their extensions
children.text: A project uses the SpecSheriff guidelines and the extensions of the guidelines it has chosen (§s-9ttvcwpqkehm58g) as the SpecSheriff plugin holds them, and makes no copy of them, unless the project is SpecSheriff itself, where they are written.
children.reason: Because they come in full with the plugin, the SpecSheriff guidelines and their extensions read the same in every project on the same release. For the same reason, they stand approved there as they were approved where they are written. A copy changed in one project would be a second version that none of their authors reads.

decisions.problem: Rules only one project's specification needed stood in the guidelines every project would share.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the SpecSheriff guidelines hold what every project shares; a project holds what only its specification needs as rules of its own, standing to them as the technical appendix stands to the base.

decisions.problem: The SpecSheriff guidelines were to name owners of their own, as a domain does, so that the confirmations they carried into a project would hold there under signatures that project's owner never gave.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the SpecSheriff guidelines are no domain and have no owners in a project; a project takes them whole, at a version its specification's owner names, their confirmations stay where they are written, and the checks compare them to that version.

decisions.problem: The part of the guidelines every project takes whole was named the core, a general word that does not say of what.
decisions.ruling: The owner: it is named the SpecSheriff guidelines.

decisions.problem: Whether a project names the version of the checks it runs, taking the tools of that version from the repository the SpecSheriff guidelines are written in into a cache on the machine, or the plugin, which Claude Code updates on each machine, carries the tools.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the plugin is a package holding everything its work needs, and every release reaches every machine through the marketplace's update; a machine not yet updated is its user's matter, and a team's CI is its own and left out of the design.

decisions.problem: Whether a project's own guidelines may hold rules tied to no rule of the SpecSheriff guidelines, provided they contradict none.
decisions.ruling: The owner: every rule of a project's own guidelines refines or implements a rule of the SpecSheriff guidelines. The link is what lets a reader judge that it contradicts none, which no check can decide, and a rule on keeping the specification that finds no parent there is most likely a rule of the product.

decisions.problem: The rule let a project's own guidelines hold a kind of node of its own, while the schema every project reads admits only the kinds it defines.
decisions.ruling: In line with the owner's ruling on §s-rah8b37kytb682y: the kinds of node are those the schema defines (§s-eferktypcj7njt5), the same in every project.

decisions.problem: The ruling of 2026-10-31 made the kinds of node the same in every project, so a project's own rules needing a kind of their own could not stand.
decisions.ruling: In line with the owner's ruling on §s-vsh384ybt4w25a2: a project's own guidelines may declare kinds of node of their own.

decisions.problem: The node named a node's status checked, the act of agreeing to it a confirmation, and one owner of a part.
decisions.ruling: Carrying out the owner's decision of that day: a node's status is draft or approved, the act is an approval, and a part has owners, one or several.

decisions.problem: The node was written before the rules of one thought to a sentence (s-juucyammgq4shq8) and of what is applied together (s-6j8ystpj2yzcchq), and before the names of the method were settled.
decisions.ruling: In the owner's name, carrying out those rules and the names the owner settled on 2026-11-07: the wording rewritten, its meaning unchanged.

decisions.problem: The node forbade every project from copying the SpecSheriff guidelines, SpecSheriff itself included, although that is where they are written.
decisions.ruling: The owner: SpecSheriff itself is the exception, since the guidelines are written there.

decisions.problem: The node did not say how a project uses the extensions it has chosen.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a project uses its chosen extensions as the SpecSheriff plugin holds them and makes no copy of them, as with the SpecSheriff guidelines. The owner chose to state this in each rule it concerns, rather than in one general rule.

tests: skills/tools/test/unit/reindex.test.ts::@spec s-bsya3febm6u64ab leaves the status of the SpecSheriff guidelines a project takes as it stands, and judges it where they are written

children.title: The archive
children.text:
The archive holds the nodes that have ever been approved and have since been removed from the specification. Such a node is placed there together with the reason for its removal. It may also name, by its sid, the node that replaces it. An archived node has no sid of its own.

A section with no node left in it is deleted outright, regardless of what cites it. So is a node that was never approved.

A node may later be deleted from the archive. A node restored from the archive returns to the specification as a new node, with a new sid.
children.reason:
The archive keeps the removed rules that the code may have implemented, so that each can be restored. It also keeps what later work can learn from them. The last wording of such a rule shows which line of reasoning or which approach to its problem proved mistaken. A node that was never approved was never implemented, and a section requires nothing, so in the archive either would only bury the rules that had to be removed.

A node may be deleted from the archive at any time, so anything relying on an archived node could break. For that reason, an archived node has no sid by which anything could name it. A sid kept in the archive could also come back into the specification in a copy of its node, and would then name two nodes. The sid of a replacement shows a reader which node replaced the rule at the time of its removal.
examples: A is archived, naming B as its replacement. Later, B is archived, naming C. A now names C.

decisions.problem: The reason referred to the specification's owner, while an approval is now given by an owner of the part of the specification that holds the node.
decisions.ruling: The owner: an owner of the node's part (§s-67vekyup7y8smap).

decisions.problem: The reason held that the archive keeps resolvable the citations in the code, the tests and the commits that implemented a removed rule, while nothing keeps a node in the archive for good.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the archive keeps a removed node for a time, so that it can be restored and so that later work learns from what was found wrong, as from a list of the defects found; a node may be deleted from it, and a link into it may then break.

decisions.problem: The node called the mark binding a symbol to the node it implements a tag.
decisions.ruling: A technical replacement following the owner's decision of that day: a tag is called SpecTag.

decisions.problem: A section confirmed under an earlier release would go to the archive when removed, while no section is approved now and an emptied section is deleted (§s-7445ahgjck2aefg).
decisions.ruling: In line with the owner's ruling on §s-9kfdycuq34beqvs: a section and a domain's header are never archived.

decisions.problem: The node was written before the rules of one thought to a sentence (s-juucyammgq4shq8) and of what is applied together (s-6j8ystpj2yzcchq), and before the names of the method were settled.
decisions.ruling: In the owner's name, carrying out those rules and the names the owner settled on 2026-11-07: the wording rewritten, its meaning unchanged.

decisions.problem: The node did not say when a section is deleted.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a section is deleted outright once no node is left in it.

decisions.problem: An archived node kept its sid, so anything could go on relying on a node that may be deleted from the archive at any time.
decisions.ruling: The owner: an archived node has no sid of its own, and its former sid is kept nowhere. A node restored from the archive returns to the specification with a new sid.

decisions.problem: An archived node could name as its replacement a node that was later removed in turn.
decisions.ruling: The owner: an archived node names as its replacement only a node of the specification. When that replacement is removed, the archived node names the replacement's own replacement instead, or none.

decisions.problem: The rule required an archived node to name as its replacement only a node of the specification, and each archived node naming a replacement to name the replacement's own replacement once that was removed in turn. No check could hold every participant to it, since the git hooks do not run `sheriff reindex`, which was to pass the replacement on.
decisions.ruling: The owner: that requirement is dropped ("I would drop this requirement altogether or make it optional; I see no particular benefit in it"). An archived node may name, by its sid, the node that replaces it, and nothing keeps that sid current. Row "A removed node that has ever been approved…" (s-qb79dcw694x2h63) of the main table of checks stays as agreed.

children.title: Contracts
children.text: What the parts of the specification share.

children.title: What the sections share is agreed in the contracts section
children.text:
The contracts section agrees on what the sections of the specification share:

- the terminology;
- the rules that bind more than one top-level section.

What only one section needs stays in that section, except a term (§s-ypa92gpcj3f5zj8).

The contracts section exists where the rules of the specification share something, such as a term. It is a section of its own within the base specification. A specification with no term and nothing else shared does not need it.
children.reason:
Sections that coin their own words, or make their own rules for the same matter, stop understanding one another.

Keeping in the contracts section only what binds more than one section keeps that section from answering for what a single section defines.

The contracts section exists only to agree on what the parts of a specification share, so a specification with nothing shared has nothing to put in it. It stands apart since it belongs to none of the others.

decisions.problem: The node did not say where the contracts section is, or whether every specification needs one.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the contracts section is a section of its own within the base specification. It exists only where the rules of the specification share something.

decisions.problem: The node held what only a specification divided into domains needs: the conventions for a domain's API, the statement that the contracts section is not a domain, a domain's RecordType and a separate document of contracts for several domains.
decisions.ruling: In line with the owner's decision that the rules not every project needs belong in extensions of the guidelines, the node speaks only of sections. Those matters move to an extension.

children.title: A term is defined once
children.text: Where a section needs terms of its own, they are added to the contracts section. An extension of the guidelines that the project has chosen (§s-9ttvcwpqkehm58g) may instead require one of the parts into which the base specification is divided (§s-qmmzf9nksfsa3qp) to define the terms that no other part of the base specification needs. Wherever it is defined, a term is defined once: one term that names two things is refused, and so are two terms that name the same thing.
children.reason: A term that is defined once, in a place where every rule that needs it can cite it, means the same thing in each of those rules.

decisions.problem: The first sentence of the rule was a prohibition rather than a statement of what to do.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the rule states what to do. Where a section needs terms of its own, they are added to the contracts section.

decisions.problem: Whether the owner agrees to proposal 2.9 of the questions about the base specification. Proposals 2.1 to 2.9, each of which carries out a decision the owner had already made, were shown on one page with each node in full.
decisions.ruling: The owner answered "but I have already made decisions on these questions": the proposal only carries out the owner's ruling of 2026-11-12 on where a term is defined when the base specification is divided into domains, so it is agreed to on the owner's behalf.

children.title: What a term states
children.text: A term only introduces an entity. What the system does is stated in rules. For example, a term names a quantity, and a rule states how it is computed.
children.reason: Behaviour written into a term applies in every rule that uses the word, yet none of them states it. Whoever reads such a rule does not see what it requires.

decisions.problem: Nothing in the guidelines said whether a term may state what the system does with the entity it names.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a term only introduces an entity, while what the system does is stated in rules. A computation is behaviour, so a rule, not a term, states how a quantity is computed.

children.title: The technical appendix
children.text: How the system is built, in addition to what the base specification says.

children.title: What the technical appendix contains
children.reason:
The appendix describes how the base specification's rules are implemented, so it makes no sense on its own. It exists to keep how the system is built apart from what the system does. With the appendix divided as the base is, a reader looks for the implementation of a rule in one place.

The accepted shortcomings are read as one list, so they are kept in one section, which spans the whole system as the stack does. A shortcoming is not how a rule is implemented but where the implementation is worse than it could be.

decisions.problem: The technical appendix had no stated place beside the domains, nothing said whether it could depart from the base specification, and its nodes were bound to no rule they implement.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the technical appendix stands outside the levels, as contracts does; it never contradicts the base specification but extends and refines it, a rule too narrow being widened in the base; every node implements a node of the base, the choices of the stack excepted; it is divided as the base is; this repository's appendix is the default implementation, an example each instance changes for itself, and it keeps its name, its being the default a detail.

decisions.problem: Nothing said what a node of the technical appendix holds beside the nodes it implements, and a draft retold the base rule it implemented while the values of its implementation had been moved into code.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a node of the appendix describes how the base nodes it implements are carried out, in enough detail to be read only one way — exact values, examples and edge cases — and never restates them, its links carrying what they state; the base answers what is done, the appendix how. Values taken from the code and a running instance while a project's existing documents are brought into the model are a departure recorded in the guide to adopting the method, not in the guidelines.

decisions.problem: The specification had no place for a problem of the implementation the owner set aside, so such a problem waited in the list of tasks as a task nobody meant to do.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the technical appendix holds a technical debt, one list of the problems of the implementation set aside, each only described as it stands; its standing there is the decision to set it aside.

decisions.problem: The rule had each node of the technical appendix implement a node of the base, its sections included, while a section requires nothing and the appendix's sections stand under the names of the domains they implement.
decisions.ruling: Following §s-7445ahgjck2aefg: a section of the technical appendix implements nothing; it stands under the name of the domain it implements.

decisions.problem: The node was written before the rules of one thought to a sentence (s-juucyammgq4shq8) and of what is applied together (s-6j8ystpj2yzcchq), and before the names of the method were settled.
decisions.ruling: In the owner's name, carrying out those rules and the names the owner settled on 2026-11-07: the wording rewritten, its meaning unchanged.

decisions.problem: The node mentioned domains and RecordType, which are defined by extensions of the guidelines that a project may not have chosen.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the rules that every project shares name neither domains nor RecordType. The mentions are removed, and the rule's meaning stays the same.

decisions.problem: A sentence defined the base specification by what it is not.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the sentence is removed.

decisions.problem: The title stated that the technical appendix is inseparable from the base specification, while the node lists what the appendix contains.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the title says what the technical appendix contains. The former title becomes the first paragraph of the node on how the appendix relates to the base specification.

children.title: How the technical appendix relates to the base specification
children.text:
The technical appendix is inseparable from the base specification.

The technical appendix never contradicts a rule of the base specification but extends and refines it. A rule too narrow for an implementation is widened in the base, and its detail goes to the technical appendix.

A node of the appendix describes how the nodes of the base specification it implements are to be carried out. It does so in enough detail to be read in only one way: exact values, examples and the edge cases of that implementation. It never restates what those nodes state.

Each node of the appendix implements at least one node of the base specification, except:

- a section, which requires nothing (§s-7445ahgjck2aefg);
- a choice covering the whole system, which goes in the section on the stack;
- the technical debt (§s-2r7k2aeyusgy6fw).
children.reason:
A part allowed to contradict the base would leave the base without force anywhere, since no rule could be relied on without reading the implementation too.

Described less exactly, a node would leave a choice to whoever implements it (§s-tj38pvm38nepaf5). Read alongside the nodes it implements, an appendix node restating them would be a second copy, and a copy drifts away from what it copies.

A node bound to the rule it implements is found when that rule changes, and is read alongside it.

decisions.problem: A proposed title suggested that the technical appendix implements the base specification, although it is the code that implements it.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the title says how the technical appendix relates to the base specification. The appendix describes the implementation, and the code implements what the appendix describes.

decisions.problem: The statement that the technical appendix is inseparable from the base specification served as the title of the node on what the appendix contains.
decisions.ruling: The owner: that statement opens this node as its first paragraph.

children.title: For a user interface, the base states what it shows, not how it looks
children.reason: The same rules can then be given a different look, with an appendix of its own. A rule that names its look goes stale when the look changes, although what the user can rely on has not.

decisions.problem: Nothing said whether the look of a user interface belongs in a rule of the base specification, and rules named column widths, where the browser keeps them and the icons of a menu.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the base specification holds what a user can rely on in any instance — what is shown, what it means, its order, its states, what can be done; the technical appendix holds how it looks and is built — placement, sizes, colours, icons, the kind of control, where a state is kept. A menu's order and nesting stay in the base, its icons go to the appendix.

decisions.problem: The rule carried an exception for a menu generated from the specification, which not every project has, and named the person using an interface by one project's term.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a project needing such an exception writes it into its own guidelines, refining this rule (§s-bsya3febm6u64ab); the rule refers to a user.

children.title: Technical debt
children.text:
The technical debt section lists the accepted shortcomings in the internal quality of the system's implementation. The system still does what the rules require. A defect is not technical debt.

The description of a shortcoming need not carry a reason. It may refine the nodes it concerns. Where the shortcoming lies in a technology the implementation uses, its description names the version of that technology it was seen in.

Being listed there is the whole of the choice to accept the shortcoming:

- no decision records that choice;
- the change that removes the shortcoming removes its description.
children.reason: Technical debt needs a place of its own, or it is forgotten.

decisions.ruling: The owner: technical debt is a shortcoming in the internal quality of the system's implementation that has been accepted on purpose. A defect is not technical debt.

decisions.ruling: The owner: an entry is the description of a shortcoming, which need not have a reason. Such a description may refine the nodes it concerns.

children.title: JSON Schema
children.text: What defines the structure of the specification, and what a project may add to it.

children.title: The structure of the specification is defined by its machine-readable schema
children.text:
The structure of every node and every file of the specification is defined by its machine-readable schema (JSON Schema). The schema is the only description of the structure. That schema is the schema of the SpecSheriff guidelines together with the schema of each extension of the guidelines that the project has chosen (§s-9ttvcwpqkehm58g) and the extension of the schema that the project's own guidelines add (§s-xm8rz4uupb73gu5).

A file that does not conform to the schema is refused. The refusal names the property that is wrong.
children.reason: A structure stated in prose can be broken without anyone noticing. Stated as a schema that every file is checked against, it cannot. Naming the property tells the file's author what to correct.

decisions.problem: The rule named the files the schema is kept in, which is the layout of one toolset rather than what the specification requires.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the guidelines apply the split between base and appendix to themselves (§s-a4rbry4hsu34hy8); where the schema is kept is described in the appendix of the tools.

decisions.ruling: The owner: a project's own guidelines add an extension to the schema, which may add only kinds of node, fields of an existing kind and properties of a file or of a link, and changes no definition of the shared schema. A field or a property needs no rule of its own, unlike a kind: it exempts nothing, and its values are wording its node's owner confirms.

decisions.ruling: The owner: this node states that the schema is the only description of the structure.

children.title: How a project may extend the schema
children.text:
In its extension of the schema, a project may add its own kinds of node, as well as properties of nodes, files and links.

A project neither changes a definition in the schema of the SpecSheriff guidelines or of an extension that the project has chosen (§s-9ttvcwpqkehm58g), nor contradicts those schemas.
children.reason: A project needs kinds of node and properties the SpecSheriff guidelines cannot foresee. An extension of the schema that changes no definition in the schema of the SpecSheriff guidelines or of a chosen extension keeps every structure they define the same in every project. So a tool relying on one of those structures is never wrong in any project.

decisions.problem: The node did not say whether a project's extension of the schema may add new kinds of link.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a project's extension of the schema may add kinds of node and properties of nodes, files and links, but not new kinds of link.

decisions.problem: The node did not say whether a project may change a definition in the schema of an extension it has chosen.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a project must not change such a definition, just as it must not change one in the schema of the SpecSheriff guidelines. The owner chose to state this in each rule it concerns, rather than in one general rule.

children.title: Links
children.text: How one node of the specification relates to another.

children.title: What a link is
children.text:
A link is a directed relation from one node to another. Every link states its meaning through its type. The types of link are:
- `implements` — the linking node states how the linked one is implemented.
- `refines` — the linking node states more precisely what the linked node states, states it for a narrower case, or extends the linked node. A node extends another when it adds a requirement on something that the other leaves open within its own subject, such as a value that the other leaves to each project. The linking node leaves every requirement of the linked node in force.
- `constrains` — the linking node states a condition the linked rule depends on.
- `exempts` — the linking node exempts the linked rule, or every rule under the linked section, from being implemented (§s-gf6n8ge4mke3pr2).
- `checks` — the linking node is a check, and it verifies that the linked rule is followed. Such a link is written by hand.
- `cites` — the linking node cites the linked one (§s-cxtt6jvhqcey2k9), and no other type says how the two relate to each other. So the linking node has no link of another type to the linked one.
- `term-relation` — the linking term (§s-khqsmy6mhejkrhg) and the linked term are bound, for as long as both exist, in the ratio the link carries (§s-bckzdwd35d2nefa).
- `uses` — what the linking term names makes use of what the linked term names while taking part in a process. The link carries no ratio. A term that only starts a process, such as an operator who starts an export, uses nothing the process uses.

An extension of the guidelines (§s-mbmnsnxenmavu3z) or a project's own guidelines (§s-u7tw6m8npxmv5tu) may define further types of link. Each such type states its meaning and contradicts no rule of the SpecSheriff guidelines.
children.reason: A link without a type records only that somebody thought of two nodes together. No check can evaluate it. No diagram can show it. A type named without its meaning is the same guess, one step removed.
examples: `uses`: a user fills in a form while signing up.

`refines`, extending a rule: a rule of a project's own guidelines lists the fixtures of the tests of a check that reads citations, a list that the rule it refines leaves to each project. The most likely mistake is an `implements` link from the project's rule: that rule does not state how the rule it refines is implemented.

children.title: Outgoing links are written
children.text: A node declares the links it makes, each naming the node it points at.
children.reason: A link says how a node bears on another, so the linking node declares it.

children.title: A cited node is also linked
children.reason:
Whoever changes a node learns what relies on it from the links pointing at it. Those links are built only from declared links, never from citations.

A node's links already name the nodes they point at. A node under it has links of its own. The nodes a built value is copied from hold the links themselves.

A node of the archive is no longer part of the specification, so a change to a node it cites breaks nothing.

decisions.problem: The rule did not say where a node keeps the link it declares for a citation.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the link is kept in the node's `refs` list, separately from the citation itself.

children.title: Incoming links are built
children.text:
The links pointing at a node are rebuilt from the links the nodes declare: every such entry is removed first and built again. They are never written by hand. They are kept in the same list as the links the node declares (§s-yku67x4mehbmv6f). Each names the node it comes from and is read from this node's end, which reverses its ratio (§s-bckzdwd35d2nefa).

A node of the archive holds no link pointing at it. No link it declares is mirrored in another node.

A node of the SpecSheriff guidelines holds only the links pointing at it from the SpecSheriff guidelines and from the appendix of the tools (§s-a4rbry4hsu34hy8). A node of an extension that the project has chosen (§s-9ttvcwpqkehm58g) holds only the links pointing at it from that extension and from the appendix of the tools.
children.reason:
A reverse link kept by hand survives the removal of its other end and then reads as a live relation. Rebuilt from scratch every time, the reverse direction is correct whatever was skipped before. Held in one list with the links the node makes, the links pointing at it show every relation of the node from where it stands. The end each entry names tells the direction.

A node of the archive is no longer part of the specification. A link built to or from it would read as a live relation.

The SpecSheriff guidelines and their extensions read the same in every project on the same release (§s-bsya3febm6u64ab). If they listed the links one project makes to them, the list would hold true for that project alone. The appendix of the tools comes with the same release, so the links it makes to them hold true in every project.

decisions.problem: A citation in a node was only a candidate for a link whose type a review was to name, a step no rule stated and nobody took, until hundreds of citations named nodes their own node held no link to, and the nodes cited showed nobody citing them.
decisions.ruling: The owner: no candidates — a node citing another declares the link to it, of the type that says how the two bear on each other or cites, and the reindex builds the side pointing at the node cited as it does for every link; a citation with no link is refused, and the links the citations lacked are written once.

decisions.problem: A project's own guidelines refine or implement rules of the SpecSheriff guidelines, which a project reads from the plugin for Claude Code and never writes, so the links pointing at those rules could not be held there; and where the SpecSheriff guidelines are written, the links its own project guidelines make would have been written into them and carried to every project.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a project's links to the SpecSheriff guidelines are one-way, as a law lists no act made under it; links in both directions stay everywhere else, between the rules of a project's specification and the nodes implementing them.

decisions.problem: The links pointing at a node are built from the links the nodes make, so they could be computed whenever they are asked for rather than stored in the node.
decisions.ruling: The owner: they stay stored in the node, so that an agent opening a node sees what depends on it without remembering to ask.

decisions.problem: A citation quoted as code was not read, so a diagram drawn in a code block, citing the nodes of each step, held no links to them; and the values gathered beside a field name nodes as a header's index does.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a node mentioned is a node linked, so `§` followed by a real sid is a citation everywhere in a node, text quoted as code included; a form of the notation with no sid after `§` cites nothing. The values gathered beside a field are left out as a header's index is, since the links stay with the nodes they copy.

decisions.ruling: In the owner's name, carrying out those rules and the names the owner settled on 2026-11-07: the wording rewritten, its meaning unchanged.

decisions.problem: The rule said which incoming links a node of the SpecSheriff guidelines holds, but not which ones a node of an extension that the project has chosen holds.
decisions.ruling: The owner chose to state this qualification in each rule that it concerns. Here, a node of a chosen extension holds only the links pointing at it from that extension, as a node of the guidelines holds only those from the guidelines.

decisions.problem: Together with the rule that puts the appendix of the tools outside the guidelines (s-a4rbry4hsu34hy8), the rule kept the links from the appendix of the tools from being mirrored in the nodes of the guidelines. The reason for the rule that the appendix implements the guidelines (s-uxtyyen92jygth4) relies on those links.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a node of the SpecSheriff guidelines, and a node of an extension that the project has chosen, also hold the links that point at it from the appendix of the tools. The appendix comes with the same release as the guidelines, so these links hold true in every project.

children.title: Links between terms
children.text: A `term-relation` link and a `uses` link bind two terms. No other type of link, not even `cites`, binds two terms of the specification: a term citing another term holds a `term-relation` or a `uses` link to it.
children.reason: A link between two terms says how the entities (§s-9w3u3wn37wksyxd) that the terms name relate, while every other type of link says how two nodes relate.

decisions.problem: The reason said that only a term names an entity, which no longer held once an entity came to mean anything that the specification defines.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the reason drops that claim and says only that a link between two terms tells how the entities they name relate. The text lacks nothing and stays as it is.

children.title: How a ratio is written
children.text: A ratio gives the multiplicity of each end in UML notation: a whole number, such as `1` or `2`, or a range of whole numbers, such as `0..1` or `1..3`, whose upper bound may be `*`, meaning no upper bound. In a range, the lower bound is not greater than the upper one. The linking term's end comes first. Read from the linked term, the ratio is reversed.
children.reason:
A ratio gives both ends because neither end's multiplicity follows from the other's. With the ends swapped, the same multiplicities mean something different, so the order is fixed.

Any multiplicity in that notation can be written, since an exact number, such as the two teams of a match, is as much a part of the relation as "one" or "many".
examples: `user 1:0..* session` says that a user has any number of sessions and that a session belongs to exactly one user.
`match 0..*:2 team` says that a match has exactly two teams and that a team plays any number of matches.

decisions.problem: A ratio could take only the multiplicities `1`, `0..1`, `1..*` and `0..*`, so an exact number, such as the two teams of a match, could not be written.
decisions.ruling: The owner agreed that a ratio may state any multiplicity in UML notation: a whole number, or a range of whole numbers whose upper bound may be `*`.
