children.title: How a rule is written
children.text: How a node of the specification is written.

children.title: The goal, the reader and the scope
children.reason: Those who write or review nodes apply the rules of this section in the same way only when they share the goal, the reader and the scope that this node sets out.

decisions.problem: The rules on how a node is written stated no common goal, reader or scope, so those who wrote or reviewed nodes could apply them in different ways.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a node of its own sets out the goal of these rules, the reader of a node, the parts of a node that the rules apply to and the terms a node may use without explaining them.

decisions.problem: It was unclear whether the rules on how a node is written apply to the citations in a node and to its examples.
decisions.ruling: The owner: citations are technical information, so these rules do not apply to them. Examples are kept in the separate `examples` property, so a rule that names only the title, the text and the reason does not apply to them either.

children.title: Understandability
children.text: Each sentence and each word can be read in only one way.

children.title: Who must act
children.text:
A rule that requires an action names its actor and says what that actor must do. An actor can be, for example, a person, a role, a part of the system or a tool. A rule that requires a property names the thing that must have it, such as a record or a node.

A description of a shortcoming in the technical debt section (§s-2r7k2aeyusgy6fw) also names an actor. The description says what that actor does while the shortcoming persists.
children.reason: Where a rule names no actor, nobody knows who must comply with it. Nobody can then be shown to have broken it.
examples: A rule says: "The operator approves each refund above the limit." The mistake closest to that case: "Each refund above the limit is approved", which does not say who approves the refund.

decisions.problem: A rule of the technical debt states what its subject does while a problem stands, which this rule's demand that a rule state what its subject must do did not admit.
decisions.ruling: Carried from the owner's ruling of the same day on the technical debt (§s-2r7k2aeyusgy6fw): the exception is written here, where the rule it narrows is read.

decisions.problem: Its examples were drawn from one project a reader of the method does not know.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the examples name what any system has — a user, an operator, a data record, a request — and nothing of one implementation; the worked example's subject stays in the example.

decisions.problem: The node was written before the rules of one thought to a sentence (s-juucyammgq4shq8) and of what is applied together (s-6j8ystpj2yzcchq), and before the names of the method were settled.
decisions.ruling: In the owner's name, carrying out those rules and the names the owner settled on 2026-11-07: the wording rewritten, its meaning unchanged.

decisions.problem: The rule also required a property to be stated in terms of what the specification declares, never in terms of what happens not to exist yet.
decisions.ruling: The owner: that paragraph is removed from the rule.

decisions.problem: The rule referred to a rule's subject, which can be read both as the grammatical subject and as the topic, and said too abstractly whom a rule binds.
decisions.ruling: The owner accepted a rule that distinguishes two cases. A rule that requires an action names its actor and what the actor must do, while a rule that requires a property names the thing that must have it.

children.title: The order of the text
children.text: A node's text opens with its main thought (§s-jrw6dhuthu4t8eq) in a short sentence. The qualifications of the main thought follow it. Two or more qualifications of the same kind, such as conditions, exceptions or steps, are set out as a bulleted list in the text. Reasoning, in which one statement follows from another, is written as prose.
children.reason: The order and layout of a node's text show how its statements relate to one another. Readers who have to work this out for themselves apply the node in different ways.
examples: A node's text does not say “the system refuses a request whose token has expired or that names a removed user”. It says “The system refuses a request in each of these cases:”, followed by the cases as a list.

decisions.problem: Agents read a rule written in long sentences of many clauses in different ways, and the rule of writing that prevents it bound one agent only, while the method reaches every project with its plugin.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a sentence of a node states one thought, a node's text opens with its main thought, and qualifications of one kind stand as a list in the text. The thresholds of a long sentence or paragraph are a signal kept in the skill spec-review, not counts in the base.

children.title: General words
children.reason: A rule has no context to show what a general word applies to. Each reader decides this for themselves, and the rule then binds each of them to the meaning they chose. Nothing in the word itself looks wrong, so each reader takes their own meaning to be the only one.
examples: A rule does not say “a limit on how many records a listing shows”, which would also let an export drop records. It says “a limit on how many records a user interface shows”.

decisions.problem: Its examples were drawn from one project a reader of the method does not know.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the examples name what any system has — a user, an operator, a data record, a request — and nothing of one implementation; the worked example's subject stays in the example.

decisions.problem: The schema of a node names several of its fields type and one kind, general words this rule keeps a name the specification defines from being.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a field of the node schema is read within the object holding it, which carries its object, so the schema keeps type and kind.

decisions.problem: The node named a kind of node "data record" and a node's place "address" or "id".
decisions.ruling: A technical replacement following the owner's decisions of that day: a data record is a RecordType, and a node's address or id is its location.

decisions.problem: The node was written before the rules of one thought to a sentence (s-juucyammgq4shq8) and of what is applied together (s-6j8ystpj2yzcchq), and before the names of the method were settled.
decisions.ruling: In the owner's name, carrying out those rules and the names the owner settled on 2026-11-07: the wording rewritten, its meaning unchanged.

decisions.problem: The rule said that a general word carries its object, and the word "object" also reads as a JSON object in the specification.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a general word is used together with what it applies to, and the rule no longer refers to an object.

decisions.problem: The rule did not say how close to a general word the thing it applies to must appear.
decisions.ruling: The owner: it appears in the same phrase as the general word, never a sentence later.

decisions.problem: The rule did not say which parts of a node it applies to.
decisions.ruling: The owner: it applies to a node's text, reason, list members and table cells, but not to its title.

children.title: Naming
children.reason: A name is read in every node that uses it, far from its definition. A reader applies those nodes correctly only if the name means the same thing in all of them.
examples: A term node titled "request" names an entity, so the rules on names apply to its title. The mistake closest to that case is to apply them to the title of a rule, such as "Limits", which names no entity.

columns.heading: The mistake closest to that case

node.text: Whoever writes a node coins a name (§s-9w3u3wn37wksyxd) for an entity only if the ordinary word for that entity also appears in the specification in another sense.
node.reason: A coined name that nobody needs suggests a special meaning to the reader that is not there. It is also one more name that every reader has to learn.

decisions.problem: The rule allowed a coined name only for a thing that is a procedure, an entity, a constant or a variable.
decisions.ruling: In line with the owner's ruling of the same day that a name refers to an entity, which is anything the specification defines, that condition is dropped, since it adds nothing.

typicalCase.text: SpecTag, the reference that binds code to a node: the word "tag" also appears in the specification in the sense of a git tag.

closestMistake.text: NodeArchive for the archive of removed nodes, though the word "archive" appears in the specification in no other sense.

node.text: A name (§s-9w3u3wn37wksyxd) says what the named entity is, in terms of how the entity is used or what it holds.
node.reason: A name that does not say what it names admits many meanings. In each node that uses such a name, it means whatever that node's context suggests.

typicalCase.text: billingAddress, for the address to which a user's invoices are sent.

closestMistake.text: userData, which says only whose data they are.

principle.text: A general word in a name

node.text: A general word (§s-me9k7g34jqb4rzn) forms a name (§s-9w3u3wn37wksyxd) only when it is combined with what it applies to.
node.reason: A name that consists only of a general word means whatever the context of each node suggests. A field called `type`, for example, held the kind of request in one log, the user's action in another and the kind of error in a third log.

typicalCase.text: userAction, for a field that holds the action a user took and is used apart from its object.

node.text:
A node that writes a property's key also names the object that the property belongs to, in one of these forms only:
- where the object's name (§s-9w3u3wn37wksyxd) is written in code font: that name, a dot and the key, all in code font, such as `TextRule.list`;
- where the object is named in ordinary words: the key in code font, with the object named in the same phrase, such as a node's `kind` or a link's `type`.

So a property's key may be a general word (§s-me9k7g34jqb4rzn). A property is given a name of its own only where it is also used apart from the object it belongs to.
node.reason: A property's key written next to the property's object means the same thing in every node, even where the key is a general word. Code font sets the key apart from the ordinary word it may coincide with.

decisions.problem: How a node writes a property's key was stated only in the spec-review skill. The ruling of 2026-10-28 made an exception for the keys `type` and `kind` without explaining it.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the specification states how a property's key is written next to the object it belongs to, so the key may be a general word. A property needs a name of its own only where it is also used apart from its object.

node.text: A node that says how one entity (§s-9w3u3wn37wksyxd) relates to another keeps the name of each and states the relation in ordinary words.
node.reason: A name coined to express a relation that an entity has to another entity reads as the name of a new entity, and the reader looks for the definition of that new entity.

closestMistake.text: SectionOwner, which reads as the name of a new entity.

decisions.problem: The rules on naming dealt with the things that names refer to, without saying what such a thing is.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a name refers to an entity, and an entity is anything that the specification defines. A name means the same thing in every node that uses it.

decisions.problem: Several principles of naming were stated only in the spec-review skill, not in the specification.
decisions.ruling: The owner: those principles move into the specification, as the rows of a table in this node, each with a rule of its own and two examples that state no requirement.

children.title: Definition by negation
children.text: A definition states what the defined thing is, never only what it is not.
children.reason: A definition by negation takes in everything it does not exclude, including what its author never meant.
examples: A definition does not say “an operator is whoever is not a user”. It says “an operator is a person who runs the system for its users”.

decisions.problem: Whether a definition may state only what the defined thing is not.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a definition by negation is not allowed. A definition states what the defined thing is.

decisions.problem: The node's text contained an example sentence.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the example goes into the node's examples, separate from its text.

children.title: Lists that restrict
children.reason: A list fails on whatever nobody thought of when it was written. One naming what is allowed shuts out every newcomer. One naming what is forbidden lets every newcomer in. For a given restriction, only one of those two mistakes is noticed.

decisions.problem: Its examples were drawn from one project a reader of the method does not know.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the examples name what any system has — a user, an operator, a record, a request — and nothing of one implementation; the worked example's subject stays in the example.

decisions.problem: The rule dealt with sets where a rule restricts something by a list, and spent its words on what everyone knows about allow-lists and deny-lists rather than on how to choose between them.
decisions.ruling: The owner: it refers to a restriction by list and keeps the criterion for choosing one.

decisions.problem: The node was written before the rules of one thought to a sentence (s-juucyammgq4shq8) and of what is applied together (s-6j8ystpj2yzcchq), and before the names of the method were settled.
decisions.ruling: In the owner's name, carrying out those rules and the names the owner settled on 2026-11-07: the wording rewritten, its meaning unchanged.

children.title: Words that take their meaning from the specification
children.text:
A node explains each word or phrase that takes its meaning from the specification, or cites the node that defines it. The explanation or the citation appears where the node first uses that word or phrase. This applies to the node's text, reason, list members and table cells.

A word or phrase takes its meaning from the specification if it is either of the following:
- a name that means something only within the specification, such as SpecTag (§s-8xw4mgvpexyvw5q);
- a common word or phrase to which the specification gives a meaning that differs from its everyday meaning, such as a narrower meaning.

Words and phrases whose definitions every reader is given are exempt (§s-qeensty237e6mmm).
children.reason: Where a word that takes its meaning from the specification is left unexplained, the reader gives it whatever meaning they know or guess. Nothing shows that meaning to be wrong, so the node is applied in a sense its writer never meant.
examples: A rule requires every test to carry a SpecTag, and cites, right after "SpecTag", the node that defines it. The mistake closest to that case: "SpecTag" appears with neither an explanation nor a citation, and only a node that the reader reaches later defines it.

A project's rule limits each user to a quota of requests, and cites, right after "quota", the term that defines a quota as the number of requests a user may send per day. The mistake closest to that case: "quota" appears with neither an explanation nor a citation, and the reader takes it in its everyday sense, a limit of any kind.

decisions.problem: The requirement that a node explain a word whose meaning the specification defines was only a personal rule of the owner, which the wording checker applied.
decisions.ruling: The owner: it becomes a rule of the specification, among the rules on clarity in the section on how rules are written.

decisions.problem: The rule did not say which words count as taking their meaning from the specification.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the rule covers a name that means something only within the specification, and a common word to which the specification gives a meaning other than its everyday one, such as a narrower meaning. A common word used in its everyday meaning is not covered.

decisions.problem: The rule gave RecordType as its example of a name that means something only within the specification, and cited a node of the RecordType extension, which a rule of the SpecSheriff guidelines does not cite (s-chk5hnzmcpeqj25).
decisions.ruling: The owner: the example is SpecTag, a name that the SpecSheriff guidelines define themselves.

children.title: One thing per unit
children.text: One thought in a sentence and one requirement in a node.

children.title: The title
children.text: A node's title says in a few words what the node is about, such as "Guaranteed fields". The text of the node states its rule. The title states only what distinguishes the node from the other nodes of its section.
children.reason: The reader sees a title first, often in a tree or in a list alongside the titles of the other nodes in the same section, and uses it to decide which node to open. A title that stated the rule would repeat the main thought that the node's text opens with.

decisions.problem: The rule on how a node's title is written was stated only among the rules for working with the owner, and nowhere in the guidelines.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the guidelines state that rule in a node of their own.

decisions.problem: The node required a title to be understood by a reader who sees nothing else.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a title is a short name for what the node is about and does not state the rule. Since the section already sets the topic, the title gives only what distinguishes the node within its section.

decisions.problem: Calling a title a short name gave the word "name" a second meaning, in addition to its meaning in the rule that one thing has one name.
decisions.ruling: The owner accepted a wording under which a title says in a few words what the node is about, and only what distinguishes it from the other nodes of its section.

children.title: Thoughts and sentences
children.reason: A sentence holding several thoughts is read in several ways. Each reader takes a different clause for the requirement and the rest for an aside.

decisions.problem: The rule did not say whether a sentence relating two facts, each of which could be disputed on its own, states one thought or two.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a sentence that states one relation between two facts, such as a cause, a contrast or a condition, states one thought. A sentence that sets two facts side by side with no relation between them, or that states two relations, states two thoughts.

children.title: The contents of a node
children.text: Requirements that a reader needs together to carry out any one of them correctly belong in one node. A requirement that can be carried out correctly without the other requirements of its node belongs in a node of its own. A main thought and its qualifications (§s-juucyammgq4shq8) are considered one requirement.
children.reason:
A rule is applied from the node it is read in. A requirement it needs that is stated in another node is missed by whoever reads the rule alone. A requirement assembled from several nodes is harder to carry out than one stated whole in one node. A main thought read without its qualifications is carried out even where they narrow it.

A node is approved, cited and bound to code as a whole. A SpecTag naming a node that contains requirements carried out separately does not say which of them the code implements.

decisions.problem: The rule of writing kept together what is applied together and said nothing of what is applied apart, while a node is approved, cited and bound to code as a whole.
decisions.ruling: The owner: requirements needed together stand in one node, and a requirement carried out rightly without the others stands in a node of its own; a main thought and its qualifications count as one requirement. The paragraph and the section, first drafted into this node, are nodes of their own by this rule.

children.title: One place for each statement
children.text: Each statement is made in one place and is not repeated.

children.title: Counts in prose
children.text:
A node states no count of what the specification or a registry holds — of nodes, of states, of members, of commands. A sentence that corrects a count states a count too.

Where the number matters, whatever holds those things produces it.
children.reason: A count is a second copy of a fact. It goes stale silently, because a number that is merely out of date looks exactly like a number that is right.
examples: A node does not say “contracts holds 45 nodes”, which was true for one day. Instead, the figure is counted from the specification's nodes each time it is shown.

decisions.problem: The node was written before the rules of one thought to a sentence (s-juucyammgq4shq8) and of what is applied together (s-6j8ystpj2yzcchq), and before the names of the method were settled.
decisions.ruling: In the owner's name, carrying out those rules and the names the owner settled on 2026-11-07: the wording rewritten, its meaning unchanged.

tests: skills/tools/test/unit/generated.test.ts::@spec s-xtqebaxjrqjsjwn sheriff guide prints every node of the guidelines and the figures counted off the model as it prints

children.title: The reason
children.text:
A reason answers why the rule exists: what it solves and what it is for. It is as short as that answer allows.

A reason speaks of the rule as a whole. It does not go through the text's paragraphs one by one and does not restate them.
children.reason: Whoever revises or approves a rule needs to know why it exists. A walk through its paragraphs does not say that.

decisions.problem: The node was written before the rules of one thought to a sentence (s-juucyammgq4shq8) and of what is applied together (s-6j8ystpj2yzcchq), and before the names of the method were settled.
decisions.ruling: In the owner's name, carrying out those rules and the names the owner settled on 2026-11-07: the wording rewritten, its meaning unchanged.

decisions.problem: Most reasons read as comments on the paragraphs of their rule's text.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a reason answers why its rule exists, what problem it solves and what it is for, as briefly as that answer allows. It concerns the rule as a whole and does not discuss the text paragraph by paragraph.

children.title: Brevity without loss of meaning
children.text: No needless rule, sentence or word.

children.title: Superfluous rules
children.reason:
A rule that does neither decides nothing.

A prohibition that no rule calls for decides nothing. Each such prohibition suggests that whatever it does not name is allowed.

A rule stating the obvious takes time to read and decides nothing either.

decisions.problem: The rule that a superfluous rule is removed stood among the rules on what the specification governs, although it concerns every rule.
decisions.ruling: The owner: it is a rule about rules in general, so it stands as a node of its own in the section on how rules are written.

children.title: The length of a sentence
children.reason: A sentence longer than its meaning requires makes the reader look for its point. A sentence shortened until it is ungrammatical can be read in more than one way. Agents then apply the rule it states in different ways.
examples: “The system, whenever a request arrives, checks the token that the request carries” becomes “The system checks the token of each request as it arrives”, not “Token check on request arrival”.

decisions.problem: The rule on keeping each sentence as short as its meaning allows was one of the owner's own rules for writing, not a rule of the guidelines.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the rule also becomes a rule of the guidelines, in a node of its own.

decisions.problem: Whether the nodes already agreed to must be rewritten at once to meet the new rule.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the rule applies to what is written from then on. An agreed node is brought into line with it when it is next changed.

decisions.problem: Read literally, the ban on replacing words with a label or an abbreviation would forbid common abbreviations, such as API, and the key `refs`, which the owner had kept as an abbreviation that misleads nobody.
decisions.ruling: The owner agreed that the ban covers only a label or an abbreviation that the specification does not define and that a reader might not know.

children.title: Rules as tables
children.reason: A `TableRule` costs more to write, read and maintain than a table in a node's text, so it is used only where a check or a node needs it.

decisions.problem: When a rule is to be made a `TableRule`, and when a cell is to hold a node rather than text.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a `TableRule`, and a node in a cell, are used only where they are needed. Elsewhere a table is written in the node's text.

children.title: Conventions of form
children.text: The language of a node, its capital letters and its examples.

children.title: The language of the specification
children.text: Every node of the specification is written in English. So is everything generated from the nodes. A quotation, such as a name from the code or text the system shows its users, matches what it quotes character for character, and so keeps its language.
children.reason:
A specification that mixes two languages, in its nodes or in what is generated from them and read instead of them, loses the distinction between what it states and what is an aside.

The language is English because a project's guidelines include the SpecSheriff guidelines, and those are written in English. A project adopts them as written and never changes them (§s-efe2cmw9asrbt2g). So a project's own nodes in another language would mix two languages in one specification.

decisions.problem: The rule named English, a choice one project made for its readers, which another project's readers need not share.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the specification is written in one language, English being recommended and holding where a project's own guidelines name no other; the SpecSheriff guidelines themselves are written in English.

decisions.problem: The rule let a project's owner name another language for the specification and required everything generated from its nodes to be in it, while a project's guidelines include the SpecSheriff guidelines, written in English, and no field held the language named for a tool to write in it the words it adds to what it generates, such as the labels of the export and of the map; and the one language held a node's quotations too, though a name from the code or a text the system shows its users may be in another.
decisions.ruling: The owner: everything of SpecSheriff is in English, every project's specification included; a quotation keeps the language of what it quotes.

decisions.problem: The node was written before the rules of one thought to a sentence (s-juucyammgq4shq8) and of what is applied together (s-6j8ystpj2yzcchq), and before the names of the method were settled.
decisions.ruling: In the owner's name, carrying out those rules and the names the owner settled on 2026-11-07: the wording rewritten, its meaning unchanged.

decisions.problem: The requirement that a quotation match what it quotes character for character was stated only in the reason, so it bound nobody.
decisions.ruling: The owner accepted moving this requirement into the text.

children.title: Capital letters
children.text:
A node is written with the ordinary capitalisation of its language. A name quoted from the code keeps its spelling.

Outside such a name, one word, or two in a row (REST API), may be set in capitals. A phrase or a sentence, three or more words in a row, is never set in capitals. What must stand out is made to stand out by the wording.
children.reason:
Set in capitals, a phrase reads as more binding than the words around it, although every word of a rule binds equally. A reader who meets capitals on every line starts reading the capitals instead of the sentence.

One or two words in capitals are most often an abbreviation or a name keeping its own spelling, which no check can tell apart from an emphasised word. So they are left alone. Three words in a row are seldom anything but emphasis. A run of abbreviations that long is rare enough to be worded around.

decisions.problem: The check refused two words in capitals running, so two abbreviations side by side, such as REST API, were refused as stress although this rule let an abbreviation keep its capitals; and a single word stressed in capitals, which this rule forbade, no check could tell from an abbreviation.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a single word, or two running, may stand in capitals; a phrase or a sentence, from three words running, never does.

decisions.problem: The node was written before the rules of one thought to a sentence (s-juucyammgq4shq8) and of what is applied together (s-6j8ystpj2yzcchq), and before the names of the method were settled.
decisions.ruling: In the owner's name, carrying out those rules and the names the owner settled on 2026-11-07: the wording rewritten, its meaning unchanged.

children.title: Examples
children.text: A node may hold examples of what its text states, in its `examples` property, separate from its text. An example shows a typical case of applying the rule and, where it helps, the mistake closest to that case. In a rule of the SpecSheriff guidelines (§s-u7tw6m8npxmv5tu) or of an extension of the guidelines (§s-mbmnsnxenmavu3z), an example may also show how a project's own guidelines could refine or extend the rule. An example imposes no requirement. Where an example and the text disagree, the text prevails.
children.reason: A reader, especially an agent, grasps a rule faster from an example of it than from its text alone. Kept apart from the text, an example neither lengthens it nor reads as a further requirement. A rule that requires only the minimum that every project needs leaves a project room to add rules of its own. Such an example shows where that room is to an agent that writes a project's own guidelines.
examples: A rule says: "The system refuses a request whose token has expired." An example of it: a request sent one second after its token expired is refused. A mistake: the request is refused and its user is signed out, which the text does not require.

decisions.problem: Whether a node must give examples of what its text states.
decisions.ruling: The owner: examples are allowed but not required. They are proposed whenever a node is written or changed.

decisions.problem: An example could show only a typical case of applying the rule and the mistake closest to that case.
decisions.ruling: The owner: in a rule of the SpecSheriff guidelines or of an extension, an example may also show how a project's own guidelines could refine or extend the rule.

children.title: Kinds of node and their location
children.text: The kinds of node and where each kind is kept.

children.title: A section contains rules and requires nothing
children.text:
A section is a node that contains a group of rules. It contains at least one rule. A section is not itself a rule.

A section's text states what the section is responsible for. The text requires nothing, since every requirement is a rule.
children.reason: Where rules need to be grouped, a section is used. It brings the rules together on a principle that the section's own text describes. A section is not itself a rule.

decisions.problem: The check of a checked section counted a data record node and a term node as its rules, while this rule named rules alone, so a section of terms, such as a glossary of contracts, passed the check and broke the rule as written.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a data record node and a term node count as rules of their section; that terms are not duplicated is held by contracts alone holding them and by no two of them sharing a name.

decisions.problem: A node of a project's own kind did not count as a rule of its section.
decisions.ruling: In line with the owner's ruling on §s-vsh384ybt4w25a2: a node of a project's own kind counts as a rule of its section.

decisions.problem: The node named a kind of node "data record" and a node's place "address" or "id".
decisions.ruling: A technical replacement following the owner's decisions of that day: a data record is a RecordType, and a node's address or id is its location.

decisions.problem: The node called the mark binding a symbol to the node it implements a tag.
decisions.ruling: A technical replacement following the owner's decision of that day: a tag is called SpecTag.

decisions.problem: The node was written before the rules of one thought to a sentence (s-juucyammgq4shq8) and of what is applied together (s-6j8ystpj2yzcchq), and before the names of the method were settled.
decisions.ruling: In the owner's name, carrying out those rules and the names the owner settled on 2026-11-07: the wording rewritten, its meaning unchanged.

decisions.problem: The node did not say plainly what a section is and what it must contain.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a section is a node that contains a group of rules. It contains at least one rule and is not itself a rule.

decisions.problem: The reason claimed that a term is named in a SpecTag, which agreed nodes contradict.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the reason says that a section groups rules where they need grouping, according to a principle that its own text describes.

children.title: What is considered a rule of a section
children.reason: Without this, a section containing only terms, nodes of a project's own kind or sections would be considered to contain no rules.

decisions.problem: The node used the name NodeKind, which nothing in the guidelines explains.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the node says "a project's own kind" instead.

decisions.problem: The node did not say for what purpose these nodes are considered rules of a section.
decisions.ruling: The owner: these nodes are considered rules of a section only for the purpose of the requirement that a section contains at least one rule.

children.title: A project's own kinds of node
children.text: A project can create nodes of any kind it needs. A project's extension of the schema (§s-xm8rz4uupb73gu5) and the project's own guidelines may declare the project's own kind of node and state whether its nodes require an implementation in code.
children.reason: A project may need kinds of node of its own, beyond those the SpecSheriff guidelines already describe.

decisions.problem: A project's own rules needed kinds of node the schema did not admit, and the rulings of 2026-10-31 had made the kinds of node the same in every project.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a project declares kinds of its own in the extension of the schema, each held as a rule is unless its nodes need no code. Whether a test is owed belongs to the code, written or generated, not to the kind, so the kind needs no more; no kind of container, since a section, to which the extension may add fields, groups nodes; each kind listed in a rule of the project's own guidelines, which its owner confirms.

decisions.problem: The node named a node's status checked, the act of agreeing to it a confirmation, and one owner of a part.
decisions.ruling: Carrying out the owner's decision of that day: a node's status is draft or approved, the act is an approval, and a part has owners, one or several.

decisions.problem: The node was written before the rules of one thought to a sentence (s-juucyammgq4shq8) and of what is applied together (s-6j8ystpj2yzcchq), and before the names of the method were settled.
decisions.ruling: In the owner's name, carrying out those rules and the names the owner settled on 2026-11-07: the wording rewritten, its meaning unchanged.

decisions.problem: The node used the name NodeKind, which says nothing by itself and which no rule explains.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the name NodeKind is removed, and the node refers to a project's own kind of node.

decisions.problem: The node implied a default value of `needsCode`, although the schema makes `needsCode` required.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the node's first sentence and its reason follow the schema, in which `needsCode` is required and has no default.

decisions.problem: The node said that a test is written before the code.
decisions.ruling: The owner: that sentence is removed, since another rule sets the order of a test and the code it tests.

decisions.problem: The node stated both that a project may declare kinds of node of its own and how such a kind is declared and checked.
decisions.ruling: The owner split the node in two. This node keeps what a project may declare, and a new node states how such a kind is declared and checked.

decisions.problem: The node only implied that a project can create nodes of any kind it needs, so its reason had nothing to refer to.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the node opens by saying that a project can create nodes of any kind it needs.

decisions.problem: Which parts of a project declare its own kind of node, and in what wording the node states what such a kind's `needsCode` determines.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a project's extension of the schema and the project's own guidelines may declare the project's own kind of node and state whether its nodes require an implementation in code. This is the wording of the node that states how such a kind is declared.

children.title: How a project's own kind of node is declared and checked
children.text:
A project adds a new kind of node to its JSON Schema, in the field `kinds` (§s-xm8rz4uupb73gu5).
Through its `schema`, a new kind of node may add fields of its own, beyond those the schema of the SpecSheriff guidelines sets for every node.
A kind's `needsCode` says whether its nodes require an implementation in code.

A rule in the project's own guidelines refines the rule on a project's own kinds of node (§s-vsh384ybt4w25a2). That rule's `TextRule.list.members` (§s-eferktypcj7njt5) holds each added kind of node with its `needsCode`. That rule's `TextRule.list.property` names the key holding a kind's name.

At each commit, a check verifies that the JSON Schema and the project's own guidelines agree on the name and `needsCode` of each new kind of node (§s-jau82aq9juv9zzh).
children.reason: Only the project knows whether the nodes of a kind it adds are carried out by code, by tools or by people. Nobody approves an extension of the schema, so this rule subjects each such kind, and whether its nodes require an implementation in code, to an owner's approval.
examples: A project adds the kind `procedure` for the steps that an operator carries out by hand. Its extension of the schema declares `"procedure": {"needsCode": false, "schema": {}}` in the field `kinds`. The rule of the project's own guidelines that refines the rule on a project's own kinds of node has `TextRule.list.property` set to `name`, and its `TextRule.list.members` holds `{"name": "procedure", "needsCode": false}`. The most likely mistake is to declare the kind only in the extension of the schema, which nobody approves.

decisions.problem: How a project's own kind of node is declared and checked was stated in a paragraph of the rule on a project's own kinds of node.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a node of its own states it, as a short account of how the mechanism works: what is new, where and how it is introduced, and what is linked to what.

decisions.problem: Where a project's own kind of node is declared, and how the rule that lists the kind refers to that declaration.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a project adds the new kind of node to its JSON Schema, in the field `kinds`. A rule in the project's own guidelines lists the kind, and that rule's `TextRule.list.declaredIn` refers to the field `kinds`.

decisions.problem: The check compared only the names of the kinds that the JSON Schema and the project's own guidelines declare, so a changed `needsCode` passed unnoticed.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the check compares both the name and the `needsCode` of each new kind of node.

decisions.problem: What a kind's `needsCode` states.
decisions.ruling: The owner: `needsCode` states whether the kind's nodes require an implementation in code.

decisions.problem: Whether the owner agrees to group 3 of stage 2 of task T25, items 27 to 32 and the owner's ruling of 2026-11-24 on comments and whitespace, shown on one page with each node in full.
decisions.ruling: The owner agreed to the group ("ok", in answer to "Do you agree to group 3?").

children.title: A node's location
children.reason: A location is computed from where a node is, so it always shows a reader where to find the node.
examples: A rule kept in `specs/_guidelines/spec.json` as the fifth node of the file's eighth section is at `_guidelines/spec/8.5`. Where an extension makes a part `requests` open with a header, the header is at `requests`, and the part's first section, kept in another of its files, is at `requests/1`. The most likely mistake is to number the header, which would put that section at `requests/2`.

children.title: A rule may be a table
children.text: A rule may be set out as a table, as a node of the kind `TableRule`. A `TableRule` has a title, a text and a reason, as a `TextRule` has. It also names its table's columns. Each cell of the table holds either text or a node of a kind that the specification's schema declares and whose nodes need no title, such as a rule. A node in a cell has no title of its own. Its column and its row name it. The rows may be grouped under headings.
children.reason: A table shows at a glance what many requirements share and where they differ. A requirement that is a node in a cell can be approved, cited and bound to code on its own.

decisions.problem: How a rule that has the form of a table is held in the specification.
decisions.ruling: The owner: each cell of the table holds either text or a node, and no separate kind of node stands for a row. The rows may be grouped under headings.

children.title: Tests and code
children.text: How a test checks a rule and how the code implements it, in the order in which they are written.

children.title: What is considered the system's code
children.text:
The system's code is the code implementing every part of the specification except its guidelines. The tests of that code are part of the system's code too. Code generated from the specification's nodes is considered code implementing the specification, like any other code.

The repository's configuration, its own tools and the tests of those tools are not part of the system's code. A project's own checks (§s-2fau85dfyyeq66m) and generators are among those tools. Whether a file is part of the system's code is decided by where it is kept.
children.reason: The rules binding code to the specification need a line between the system's code and whatever supports the work on the system. Tests are written before the code, and the code must conform to them (§s-rah8b37kytb682y). So the tests cannot be separated from the code and fall on its side of that line. A file's location is the same for every check, so the location draws that line.

decisions.problem: Nothing said what the system's code is, while the base names it throughout, and the repository's tools, its configuration and every test were exempt from tags by where they live.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the system's code is the code implementing the specification, its tests included, since they are written first; the repository's configuration, its own tools and their tests are not.

decisions.ruling: A technical replacement following the owner's decision of that day: a tag is called SpecTag.

decisions.ruling: A technical replacement in line with the owner's rulings of the same day on a test's SpecTag and on a draft: a test names its node by its SpecTag, and the check that binds symbols to their nodes reads only the symbols of code other than tests.

decisions.problem: The node was written before the rules of one thought to a sentence (s-juucyammgq4shq8) and of what is applied together (s-6j8ystpj2yzcchq), and before the names of the method were settled.
decisions.ruling: In the owner's name, carrying out those rules and the names the owner settled on 2026-11-07: the wording rewritten, its meaning unchanged.

decisions.problem: The node did not say clearly which parts of the specification the system's code implements, or why the tests belong to that code.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the system's code is the code implementing every part of the specification except its guidelines, not only the code written by hand. Its tests belong to it, since they are written before the code and the code must conform to them.

children.title: The implementation of an approved rule
children.reason: An approved rule that the system's code does not implement leaves the specification stating something that is not true of the system.

decisions.problem: Nothing reported a checked rule that the system's code did not carry out: a test was required only once a commit changed a rule's code, so a rule nobody reached stood unnoticed while the specification stated it.
decisions.ruling: The owner: every checked rule is implemented — a symbol of the system's code tagged with it and a passing test carrying its sid, a tag or a test of a rule implementing it counting — or is exempted by a node of the project's own guidelines with an exempts link; the SpecSheriff guidelines, the project's own guidelines and the technical debt are outside it, where the guidelines are written as well.

decisions.ruling: In line with the owner's ruling on §s-vsh384ybt4w25a2: a node of a project's own kind is implemented as a rule is, unless its kind needs no code, and is exempted as a rule is.

decisions.ruling: In line with the owner's ruling on §s-hheus6f395ynqvc: in the repository in which the guidelines are written, the code of the SpecSheriff tools is not the system's code.

decisions.problem: The node did not say whether code or a test bound to a node that implements an approved rule counts towards that rule.
decisions.ruling: The owner: such code or such a test counts towards the rule, whether the node implements the rule directly or through a chain of `implements` links.

children.title: The SpecTag
children.text: A SpecTag binds a rule to the code that implements it and to the tests written for it.
children.reason: Whether a rule is implemented is determined by its code and a passing test together (§s-6fw72j65jkqrfpf). A reference to the rule, written the same way in both, lets that be read off the code and the tests themselves.

decisions.problem: Two nodes, one on a test's SpecTag and one on the SpecTag of technical code, each stated part of what a SpecTag is for.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the two nodes become one, which states only what a SpecTag is for. A SpecTag binds a rule to the code that implements it and to the tests written for it.

children.title: Which edits change a test or code
children.reason: Tests and code that change are checked again against the rules their SpecTags name. This rule draws the line between an edit to a test or code that can affect that check and one that cannot.
examples: A commit re-indents a block of TypeScript code, adds a comment above it and changes nothing else, so the commit changes no code. By contrast, a commit that indents a key of a YAML file further, which nests the key under the key above it, changes the code.

decisions.problem: The node said that rewriting a test's reference to its node, in another form that names the same node, changes no test.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a SpecTag must stay the same, not merely name the same node, so a SpecTag rewritten in another form is a change.

decisions.problem: Two nodes, one on binding a test to an approved rule and one on the code that must name an approved node, each determined in part whether a SpecTag changes.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the two become one node, titled "A change to a SpecTag".

decisions.problem: The node did not say which edits leave a test or code unchanged.
decisions.ruling: The owner: as long as the SpecTag stays the same, renaming a test or rewording the comments in the code and the tests changes neither the test nor the code.

decisions.problem: The node did not say whether a change to a SpecTag changes the whole file it is in or only part of it.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a change to a SpecTag is a change to the test or the code that the SpecTag binds. That is the symbol beneath it, or the whole file where the file is bound as a whole.

decisions.problem: Whether the owner agrees to group 3 of stage 2 of task T25, items 27 to 32 and the owner's ruling of 2026-11-24 on comments and whitespace, shown on one page with each node in full.
decisions.ruling: The owner agreed to the group ("ok", in answer to "Do you agree to group 3?").

children.title: Code and tests that no SpecTag binds
children.reason: Code and tests written before their rules may have no SpecTag that binds them and still work correctly. Refusing every commit while such code exists would stop all work until all of it was bound to rules. So the owners decide when such code is reported, by approving the specification, and when it must be bound, by turning its `strict` flag on.
examples: The specification is approved, and its `strict` flag is off. A commit changes one file, whose symbols all carry SpecTags, while two old files elsewhere carry none. The commit passes, and the checks warn once that no SpecTag binds some code outside the commit, naming the command that lists that code. Were the specification a draft, the same commit would pass with no warning. The most likely mistake is to refuse the commit because of the two old files, or to list their symbols in the warning.

An old function carries a SpecTag that names the section holding the rules it implements. That SpecTag binds nothing, so while the specification is approved and its `strict` flag is off, a commit that leaves the function unchanged passes with the warning. The most likely mistake is to treat the function as bound because it carries a SpecTag.

decisions.problem: A project adopting the method with code it already has could not commit while its rules were agreed, since every untagged symbol was refused and a tag added had to name a checked node.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a project's specification is a draft or live; first, a draft relaxed every check binding the code, then, the reviewer apart finding that against two principles, narrowed: a draft relaxes only the refusal of an untagged symbol a commit does not change, which is reported; a changed symbol is held as when live.

decisions.problem: The system's code came to include its tests, which carry a sid rather than a tag.
decisions.ruling: In line with the owner's ruling on §s-hheus6f395ynqvc: the node refers to a symbol of the system's code other than tests.

decisions.problem: The node called the mark binding a symbol to the node it implements a tag.
decisions.ruling: A technical replacement following the owner's decision of that day: a tag is called SpecTag.

decisions.problem: A project holding tests could commit nothing, its setup included, before every test named a node, though a draft relieved code without a SpecTag.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a draft is above all work on the specification, the code and the tests secondary in it; a test a commit does not change and that names no node is reported rather than refused, as code without a SpecTag is.

decisions.problem: The node named a node's status checked, the act of agreeing to it a confirmation, and one owner of a part.
decisions.ruling: Carrying out the owner's decision of that day: a node's status is draft or approved, the act is an approval, and a part has owners, one or several.

decisions.ruling: In the owner's name, carrying out those rules and the names the owner settled on 2026-11-07: the wording rewritten, its meaning unchanged.

decisions.problem: Whether the rule on code and tests without a SpecTag moves to an extension for adopting an existing project or stays in the base.
decisions.ruling: The owner: it stays in the base, in the section on tests and code, next to the nodes on the SpecTag.

decisions.problem: The rule applied only while the specification was a draft, and the checks reported each symbol without a SpecTag.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the rule no longer depends on the specification being a draft. Instead of a message for each symbol, the checks issue a single warning, with no list, that names the command that lists such code by file and symbol.

decisions.problem: When the checks warn about code outside the commit that carries no SpecTag, and when they refuse the commit.
decisions.ruling: The owner: while the specification is a draft, the commit passes without a warning. While it is approved, the commit passes with the warning if the strict flag is off, and is refused if the flag is on.

children.title: The nodes a commit message names
children.text: For each node to which a SpecTag binds code added or changed in a commit, the commit message names the node by its sid. Code in the tests is not counted.
children.reason: The code's behaviour changes only as a result of a change to the specification (§s-4gk82vt7zhzp4jt). The commit message records which nodes the changed code implements, for whoever reads the history.

decisions.problem: A commit changing a domain's code named the domain's header, which says nothing of what the commit changed, and the check of the message accepted it, since any node that exists was accepted.
decisions.ruling: The owner: code changes only through the specification. A commit names the checked rules it serves, the tags of the declarations it changes name those rules, and a header or a section never stands in for a rule.

decisions.ruling: A technical replacement following the owner's decision of that day: a tag is called SpecTag.

decisions.ruling: A technical replacement in line with the owner's rulings of the same day on a test's SpecTag and on a draft: a test names its node by its SpecTag, and the check that binds symbols to their nodes reads only the symbols of code other than tests.

decisions.ruling: Carrying out the owner's decision of that day: a node's status is draft or approved, the act is an approval, and a part has owners, one or several.

decisions.ruling: In the owner's name, carrying out those rules and the names the owner settled on 2026-11-07: the wording rewritten, its meaning unchanged.

decisions.problem: The node made the commit the subject of the rule, stated one requirement twice with different scopes, and listed cases that restated the rule on the direction of change.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the node states a single requirement, on the commit message. The message names, by its sid, each node bound by a SpecTag to code that the commit adds or changes.

decisions.problem: The node referred to a symbol, although code may also be bound to a node as a whole file.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the node refers to code that a SpecTag binds, rather than to a symbol.

children.title: A node's lists of its code and its tests
children.text:
The SpecSheriff tools build a node's `meta.code` and `meta.tests` from the SpecTags that bind code and tests to it. They rebuild them after every edit to the code, the tests or the specification. Nobody writes them by hand.

In a node of the SpecSheriff guidelines or of an extension of the guidelines (§s-mbmnsnxenmavu3z), the SpecSheriff tools list only the code and the tests of the repository where the guidelines are written.
children.reason: A node's lists show the code that implements the node, and the tests written for it, to a reader who has the node open. Built from the SpecTags, they cannot fall out of step with the code the way a list kept by hand does.

decisions.problem: A test bound to its rule by the opening of its name cannot be written in a language whose names cannot hold a hyphen.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a test declares the sid of what it verifies however its language allows, so that a run of the tests reports it.

decisions.problem: The node called the mark binding a symbol to the node it implements a tag.
decisions.ruling: A technical replacement following the owner's decision of that day: a tag is called SpecTag.

decisions.problem: A symbol named its node by a SpecTag while a test opened its name with the bare sid or held it in a mark: two forms of one reference.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a test declares its node by a SpecTag too, standing where the bare sid stood, so that every binding of code or a test to a node takes one form and a run of the tests still shows it.

decisions.problem: The node was written before the rules of one thought to a sentence (s-juucyammgq4shq8) and of what is applied together (s-6j8ystpj2yzcchq), and before the names of the method were settled.
decisions.ruling: In the owner's name, carrying out those rules and the names the owner settled on 2026-11-07: the wording rewritten, its meaning unchanged.

decisions.problem: The node required a node's lists of code and tests to be written by hand and to agree with the SpecTags.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the SpecSheriff tools build these lists from the SpecTags and rebuild them after every edit. Nobody writes them by hand.

decisions.problem: The node did not say which code and tests the lists name in a node of an extension that a project has chosen.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the lists in such a node name only the code and the tests of the repository where the guidelines are written, as in a node of the SpecSheriff guidelines. The owner chose to state this in each rule it concerns, rather than in one general rule.

children.title: Exempting a rule from being implemented
children.text:
A node of a project's own guidelines exempts a rule from being implemented, including a rule of a project's own kind of node. It does so by a link of type `exempts` (§s-sn6au3vcr9uy5pm) to one of these:
- that rule;
- a section the rule is under, at any depth.

The exempting node says in its own text why the exemption is made.

An `exempts` link is allowed only where the exempting node's text cites its target. An exemption holds only while the exempting node is approved.
children.reason: A rule that the system's code cannot implement, or that no test can verify, would be reported as unimplemented for as long as it exists. Lifting the requirement that a rule be implemented is an owner's decision (§s-67vekyup7y8smap). An approval covers a node's wording and not its links (§s-5ah25f6gy99panq). So an exemption holds only where approved wording names what it exempts.

decisions.problem: An exemption made by a link alone would hold even though no approved wording names what it exempts, since an approval does not cover links.
decisions.ruling: The owner: an `exempts` link is allowed only where the exempting node's text cites its target. An exemption holds only while the exempting node is approved.

decisions.problem: The node exempted "a rule, or a node of a project's own kind", as though a node were something other than a rule.
decisions.ruling: The owner: code implements a rule, and a node is only the form in which a rule is kept. So the node is about exempting a rule, including a rule of a project's own kind of node.

decisions.problem: A sentence requiring the exempting node's text to cite each rule or section it exempts repeated the next sentence. For a section, it also seemed to require citing every rule under it.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the sentence is removed.

children.title: The checks and the procedures
children.text: How a change to the specification or the code is checked, and how the procedures that SpecSheriff provides behave.

decisions.problem: Whether the owner agrees to wording 3.1 of the questions about the base specification. The new wordings 3.1 and 3.3 to 3.8 were shown on one page with each node in full.
decisions.ruling: The owner agreed ("agreed", in answer to "Do you agree to the wordings of 3.1 and 3.3–3.8?").

children.title: The main table of checks
children.text: This table contains the complete list of the checks of the SpecSheriff guidelines that run after an edit to the specification or to the code, including its tests.
children.reason: In one table, every check can be seen at a glance, together with what its failure costs. Gathered in one place, the checks are easier to read and to compare with one another than when spread across separate rules.

node.text: No object in a file of the specification, of its archive or of its schema assigns two values to one property
node.reason: Where one property is given two values, a JSON parser silently keeps one of them. The SpecSheriff tools then read something other than what the file says.

node.text: Every file of the specification complies with its JSON Schema

decisions.problem: The check said only that every file matches its schema, without saying which files or which schema.
decisions.ruling: The owner worded the check: every file of the specification complies with its JSON Schema.

node.text: No two nodes of the specification share a sid
node.reason: A node is cited by its sid, so a sid that two nodes shared would name both of them.

decisions.problem: Whether the check that no two nodes share a sid covers the nodes in the archive.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the check covers only the nodes of the specification, since an archived node keeps no record of its former sid.

node.text: The location of each node of the specification names where that node is in the specification

decisions.problem: An archived node keeps the location it had when it was removed, and another node may later take that location.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the check covers only the nodes of the specification. It makes the check that no two nodes share a location redundant, and that check is therefore removed.

node.text: Every term node of the specification is in the contracts section, or in a part of the base specification where a chosen extension of the guidelines allows terms to be defined (§s-ypa92gpcj3f5zj8)

decisions.problem: An archived term node is in the archive rather than in the contracts section.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the check covers only the term nodes of the specification.

decisions.problem: Where a term is defined when the base specification is divided into domains.
decisions.ruling: The owner agreed to the check as it applies to a base specification without domains. The extension for domains extends it: a term that several domains need is defined in the contracts section, and a term that one domain needs is defined in that domain.

decisions.problem: Whether the owner agrees to proposal 2.9 of the questions about the base specification. Proposals 2.1 to 2.9, each of which carries out a decision the owner had already made, were shown on one page with each node in full.
decisions.ruling: The owner answered "but I have already made decisions on these questions": the proposal only carries out the owner's ruling of 2026-11-12 on where a term is defined when the base specification is divided into domains, so it is agreed to on the owner's behalf.

node.text: No two term nodes of the specification name the same term, regardless of letter case

decisions.problem: Applied to the archive, the check would keep a new term from taking the name of a term that has been removed.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the check covers only the term nodes of the specification, so a new term may take the name of an archived one.

decisions.problem: The check required an approval of every node outside the SpecSheriff guidelines, including the nodes of the extensions of the guidelines that the project has chosen.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the check also leaves out the nodes of the extensions that the project has chosen.

decisions.problem: Whether the owner agrees to group 1 of stage 2 of task T25, the checks that `sheriff validate` runs, shown on one page with each node in full, and to option A in both of the group's questions.
decisions.ruling: The owner agreed to the group and to option A in both questions ("ok", in answer to "Do you agree to group 1 and to option A in both questions?").

node.text: Each approval added in a commit names one of the owners of its node as of that commit

decisions.problem: The check treated the commit itself as the one that approves, and covered every approval, not only those that the commit adds.

children.title: An agent's edit is checked before it is made
children.reason: A check that runs later sees only the result: the approvals, which it takes as given, and a commit that contains a test together with the code it tests. decisions.ruling: The owner: where an agent writes, the checks run at each of its edits, and an edit that would leave a node checked unconfirmed or change the code of a rule with no test is refused before it is made; the hooks ship with the tools and are kept in git.

decisions.problem: An agent could write a confirmation of a new wording into the confirmations and then reword a checked node: the check before the edit found the confirmation and let the edit pass, and only this rule's reason spoke against it.
decisions.ruling: The owner: an agent's edit changing the confirmations is refused before it is made; only the procedure that records a confirmation or withdraws one writes them.

decisions.problem: The reason held that nobody but a node's owner confirms it, while the agent working for the owner may now confirm in the owner's name a node whose change states nothing new.
decisions.ruling: In line with the owner's ruling on §s-67vekyup7y8smap: the reason names this exception: the agent approves on the owner's behalf a node whose change states nothing new.

children.title: What the reviewer is given
children.reason: The reviewer makes the judgements that no deterministic check can make: whether code does only what its rules say, whether a comment agrees with the code and its rules, whether a rule's implementation really needs no change, and whether an approved node of the technical appendix agrees with the base specification. It can judge only from what it is shown. Shown what each judgement needs, and nothing about what the author of the change meant, it judges by the rules alone.

decisions.problem: The reviewer was given the rules a commit names and no data record, so code generated from a data record had nothing to be read against, and the definition of a term the code's names follow was withheld; a generated data record was refused field by field as stated by no rule.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the reviewer is given the rules, data records and terms the message and the tags name, a data record with its fields.

decisions.problem: The reviewer was one agent's command line, so the method read as one vendor's tool, and a reader without that agent could not run it.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the base states the reviewer's contract; who carries the review out is a runner described in the appendix of the tools, and a review that cannot be held refuses the commit.

decisions.problem: The types and runtime checks generated from a project's data records are its code, so a commit adding them is reviewed, but they were left out of the change the reviewer was given without its being told so: given a message naming the data records and a change holding none of their types, the reviewer refused the commit as leaving them out.
decisions.ruling: The owner: each file left out is named to the reviewer as holding the types and runtime checks generated from the data records, which the check of the generated copies compares with what the nodes produce, and what a data record requires counts as carried out by them.

decisions.problem: The reviewer was given the fields of a data record but not those of a node of a project's own kind.
decisions.ruling: In line with the owner's ruling on §s-vsh384ybt4w25a2: the reviewer is given the fields of a node of a project's own kind as well.

decisions.problem: The reviewer was told only of the files holding the types and runtime checks of data records.
decisions.ruling: In line with the owner's ruling on §s-km4x4s26kv7pjze: the reviewer is told what a project's generator wrote, and counts what the generator's rule says the generator writes as carried out by the generator.

decisions.problem: The reviewer was given a node's text without its reason, which the tools gave before their rewrite.
decisions.ruling: The owner: it is given each node's reason too, and refuses only what no named node's text states.

decisions.problem: The node named a kind of node "data record" and a node's place "address" or "id".
decisions.ruling: A technical replacement following the owner's decisions of that day: a data record is a RecordType, and a node's address or id is its location.

decisions.problem: The node called the mark binding a symbol to the node it implements a tag.
decisions.ruling: A technical replacement following the owner's decision of that day: a tag is called SpecTag.

decisions.problem: The node named a test's reference to its node a sid, or read a SpecTag as standing only on a symbol, once a test came to carry a SpecTag too.
decisions.ruling: A technical replacement in line with the owner's rulings of the same day on a test's SpecTag and on a draft: a test names its node by its SpecTag, and the check that binds symbols to their nodes reads only the symbols of code other than tests.

decisions.problem: The node was written before the rules of one thought to a sentence (s-juucyammgq4shq8) and of what is applied together (s-6j8ystpj2yzcchq), and before the names of the method were settled.
decisions.ruling: In the owner's name, carrying out those rules and the names the owner settled on 2026-11-07: the wording rewritten, its meaning unchanged.

decisions.problem: Who verifies a commit message's statement that a rule's implementation needs no change.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the independent reviewer verifies it, and the principle on deterministic checks is extended to say so.

decisions.problem: Who checks a node of the technical appendix that an agent approved on an owner's behalf.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the independent reviewer checks it, in the commit in which the node is approved, whoever approved it.

decisions.problem: Which rules of the base specification the reviewer is given with a node of the technical appendix, since the person who commits pays for the reviewer's tokens.
decisions.ruling: The owner chose the rules the node implements, the rules linked to them in either direction, and the rules in the same top-level section of the base specification, rather than only the linked rules or the whole base specification.

decisions.problem: The node said that the reviewer is given the nodes that the code implements.
decisions.ruling: The owner: code implements rules, so the node refers to the rules that the code implements.

decisions.problem: Whether the owner agrees to group 2 of stage 2 of task T25, the reviewer's check of a commit and the SpecTag in code and in tests, shown on one page with each node in full.
decisions.ruling: The owner agreed to the group ("agreed", in answer to "Do you agree to group 2?").

decisions.ruling: The owner agreed to the group ("ok", in answer to "Do you agree to group 3?").

children.title: Who chooses an agent's model and reasoning effort
children.reason: Whoever runs an agent pays for that run, so only they decide what it costs.
examples: A skill of a SpecSheriff plugin starts an agent to review a draft. That agent uses the model and the reasoning effort of the session in which the skill runs. The most likely mistake is a skill that names a model or a reasoning effort of its own, so that the person pays for a model or a reasoning effort that they did not choose.

decisions.problem: Whether the owner agrees to proposal 3.2 of the questions about the base specification, the rule on who chooses an agent's model and reasoning effort.
decisions.ruling: The proposal was taken off the owner's page because it only carries out the owner's decision of 2026-11-02 that no choice that costs a user tokens is made without their consent, so it is agreed to on the owner's behalf.

children.title: A commit whose review cannot be carried out is refused
children.text: The SpecSheriff tools refuse a commit for which the reviewer must make at least one judgement other than the one on comments (§s-m4h279nbaqkpa3t) unless the reviewer gives an answer that the tools can read. The refusal says why the review could not be carried out. Where the commit needs only the judgement on comments, the tools issue a warning that says why the review could not be carried out.
children.reason: A review that lets a commit through whenever it could not be carried out is a review nobody can rely on.
examples: No reviewer is installed.
The reviewer's run does not end within its time limit.
The run ends with an error.
The answer passes the commit but reports a finding on code.

children.title: The specification's approval status
children.text:
Only an owner of the specification approves it or returns it to draft. That owner records each such act in a separate entry, which names that owner. Only the latest such entry determines the specification's approval status.

Before the approval procedure records an approval of the specification, it runs the checks listed in the main table of checks (§s-jau82aq9juv9zzh) or in the table of checks of an extension. It skips the review and the checks that need a commit message or a run of the tests. It runs the others as if the specification were approved and one commit added the whole specification and all of the system's code (§s-hheus6f395ynqvc). It shows the approving owner what they find, for example a symbol that no SpecTag (§s-8xw4mgvpexyvw5q) binds or an approved rule that has no test or no code. If the checks find anything, the procedure records the approval only after the owner confirms the approval. While the specification's `strict` flag is on, the procedure refuses to record the approval in the cases that the rule on that flag names (§s-q3pfzyaxvpr2zj2).
children.reason:
Whether the specification is approved determines whether the tests must pass before a change reaches the project's shared branch (§s-m4h279nbaqkpa3t). So its owners decide it, in both directions, by an act of their own.

The owners may need to return the specification to draft for any reason. While the specification is changing fundamentally, for example when another version of it is adopted or the system's architecture changes, the code and the tests are secondary.

Approving the specification is a decision of its own, separate from approving any rule. Were the specification's approval status tied to a rule, anyone editing that rule would change it.

The owners base their decision on what they see. Old code that no SpecTag binds may still work correctly, so while the `strict` flag is off, such code does not block the approval. The checks that run at a commit judge only what the commit contains, so they never show everything that the specification and the code still lack. Seeing what is missing, the owners approve the specification deliberately rather than by oversight.
examples: Every rule of the specification is approved, but none of its owners has approved the specification. The specification is a draft. But not: the specification is approved because all its rules are, as a section would be.

The specification's `strict` flag is off. Two symbols of old code have no SpecTag. An owner starts the approval procedure, sees the two symbols listed, confirms, and the specification is approved. But not: the procedure refuses to approve the specification until every symbol has a SpecTag.

children.title: The specification's strict flag
children.text:
The specification has a `strict` flag. A rule of the SpecSheriff guidelines, of an extension of the guidelines (§s-mbmnsnxenmavu3z) or of a project's own guidelines (§s-u7tw6m8npxmv5tu) may make a check (§s-jau82aq9juv9zzh) stricter while the flag is on.

Only an owner of the specification turns the `strict` flag on or off. That owner records each such act in a separate entry, which names that owner. Only the latest such entry determines the `strict` flag.

The following procedures refuse to run while a check that the `strict` flag makes stricter would refuse a commit or a push that changes nothing, if the specification were approved and the flag were on:
- the procedure that turns the `strict` flag on;
- the procedure that approves the specification, while the `strict` flag is on (§s-qzthyh7yqvfhsa2).

Each refusal names the command of the SpecSheriff tools that lists what that check finds.
children.reason: The rules of the guidelines require only the minimum that every project needs. Some projects need stricter checks: for example, a project all of whose code is bound to its rules and has to stay that way. The `strict` flag lets the owners make the checks stricter by an act of their own, without stopping all work when they do.
examples: The specification is approved, and its strict flag is on. Under the rule on code that no SpecTag binds (§s-kkbqcb9xrpaepwn), code that a commit does not change and that no SpecTag binds makes the checks refuse the commit. An earlier commit, made with the git hooks bypassed, added a file whose symbols carry no SpecTags. The next commit, which changes another file whose symbols all carry SpecTags, is refused, and the refusal names the command that lists the symbols of the added file. But not: that commit passes with a warning, as it would with the flag off.
A project's own guidelines may refine one of the project's own checks (§s-2fau85dfyyeq66m) so that, while the flag is on, it refuses a commit in a case where it would otherwise only report.

decisions.problem: The owners had no means of making the checks refuse a commit while code that the commit leaves unchanged carries no SpecTag.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the specification has a `strict` flag at the same level as its approval status. Only an owner changes the flag, by a separate entry, and its default value, false, is set only by the schema.

decisions.problem: What happens when an owner turns the flag on, or approves the specification while the flag is on, and code without a SpecTag remains.
decisions.ruling: The owner: both procedures refuse to run, and each refusal names the command that lists the code without a SpecTag, instead of listing that code itself.

decisions.ruling: The owner: the flag keeps the name `strict` and is not limited to code without a SpecTag: a rule of the SpecSheriff guidelines, of an extension or of a project's own guidelines may make any check stricter while the flag is on. Both refusals then apply to every check that the flag makes stricter.
